item.title: Breaking Down the Ending of Agent Kim Reactivated
item.description: The thrilling action series follows an unassuming single dad who reveals his past as a secret agent when his daughter disappears

media:content.media:description: So Ji-sub

item.content:encoded:
Agent Kim Reactivated, a Korean drama broadcast on SBS TV domestically and streamed on Netflix globally, has become one of the summer’s biggest hits. The thrilling action series follows an unassuming bank manager and single dad named Kim (So Ji-sub). When his teen daughter, Min-ji (Seo Su-min), disappears after a fight at school, Kim’s background and skillset as a secret agent is revealed as he stops at nothing to find her. 

Agent Kim is aided by his two friends: taekwondo instructor Sung Han-soo (Choi Dae-hoon) and boisterous military man Park Jin-cheol (Yoon Kyung-ho). Like Agent Kim, Han-soo and Jin-cheol are former spies and current parents. In an effort to rescue Min-ji, the three middle-aged, bespectacled dads face off against criminal organizations and state intelligence entities as what starts as a clash between two teenagers disturbs a decade-long lull in intergovernmental espionage. The 10-episode drama about paternal anxiety and devotion wrapped up over the weekend. Here’s everything that happened in the final episodes of Agent Kim Reactivated.

Does Min-ji die?

The first few episodes of Agent Kim Reactivated imply that Kim’s beloved daughter Min-ji  has died. At the end of Episode 1, Hye-ri (Yoo Ji-an), Min-ji’s classmate and the daughter of Juhak Construction group chairman Ju Gang-chan (Joo Sang-wook), hits Min-ji over the head with a brick. Min-ji loses consciousness, leading Hye-ri and Min-ji’s other bullies to assume she is dead. A panicked Hye-ri convinces local thug Golden Teeth (Jo Bok-rae) to take care of the body. 

However, unbeknownst to both Hye-ri and Golden Teeth, Min-ji has survived the attack. She later wakes up in the cold storage warehouse where Golden Teeth has temporarily stashed her “body”, and escapes. This is just the beginning of Min-ji’s many efforts to get back to her father. Next, she is picked up by Ju Gang-chan while trying to hitchhike. Then, she is “rescued” by South Korea’s Special Missions Directorate (SMD), where director Kang Guk-cheol (Won Hyun-joon) ties her up and questions her for information about her father. It’s a foolish strategy. Agent Kim has kept his daughter in the dark about his dark past.

Agent Kim’s secret past

Agent Kim was born in North Korea, and was trained from a young age to be a special operative for his native government. However, when Kim is captured during a failed mission in South Korea, he has a choice to make: be disappeared by the SMD, or agree to work for them. He chooses the latter, and becomes friends with operatives Han-soo and Jin-cheol through their missions together.

Kim also meets and falls in love with a South Korean woman. When she dies in childbirth, he forces his retirement from the SMD in order to raise his baby. The SMD allows his freedom on one condition: he must lay low. If the North Korean government realizes their former operative is alive in South Korea, it will cause an international incident. 

Kim gladly devotes himself to a quiet life as a father and office worker, and the SMD leaves him alone. But when Min-ji goes missing and Kim starts wreaking havoc across the city looking for her, North Korean Intelligence learns of his continued existence. The SMD and North Korean Intelligence both set out to capture Agent Kim. 

Who is Agent 66?

The pseudonym “Agent 66” is first used by Park Yeong-gwang (TaecYeon), a North Korean spy who trained alongside Agent Kim. When Yeong-gwang dies during his and Agent Kim’s first mission to South Korea, betrayed by the North Korean agency that sent them, Agent Kim takes on the moniker.

When Agent Kim reappears on the North Korean government’s radar after years of being presumed dead, Park Yeong-gwang’s little brother, Gang Seong (Kim Sung-kyu), is sent to kill him. He too uses the name “Agent 66” as his codename. Though killing Kim may be Gang Seong’s orders, the mission is also personal for the new Agent 66, who has been told that Kim is responsible for the death of his big brother. When Kim dispels this lie, revealing that it was North Korean intelligence director Ri Eung-ryeong who betrayed them all, Gang Seong abandons his mission to kill Kim. 

Later, after Ri Eung-ryeong spills his secrets to the South Korean government in exchange for asylum, Agent Kim kidnaps and hands Ri Eung-ryeong over to Gang Seong. Gang Seong brings Ri Eung-ryeong back to North Korea, where he is presumably punished for his defection.

The ending of Agent Kim Reactivated

Heading into the season finale, Agent Kim has managed to evade SMD capture by protecting defector Ri Eung-ryeong during the intergovernmental talks between North Korea and South Korea. With the completion of one final mission for the SMD, Kim has earned his freedom (again) and the promise of a normal life with Min-ji. He just has to stay alive to claim it. And, unfortunately, Ju Gang-chan—the former thug turned Juhak Construction chairman—is still gunning for him. He wants to see Agent Kim, Han-soo, and Jin-cheol suffer for besting him. To do so, Ju Gang-chan kidnaps Han-soo and Jin-cheol’s children. He holds the teens at gunpoint and forces Han-soo and Jin-cheol to fight Agent Kim.

The three friends initially go along with Ju Gang-chan’s orders to kill Agent Kim, but use their years of experience working together to come up with an out. They lure a boasting Ju Gang-chan closer to the fence of the cage in which they are fighting, and manage to knock it down onto the villain. They rescue their children, and hand Ju Gang-chan over to the authorities. Later, he is stabbed multiple times by Golden Teeth while being transported out of the hospital. Hye-ri, the spoiled daughter whose bullying acted as a catalyst for this entire sequence of events, has been sent abroad following the public humiliation of her family.

Agent Kim and Min-ji are reunited

The father-daughter relationship between Agent Kim and Min-ji is at the heart of Agent Kim Reactivated, and it’s at the heart of the finale, too. Following the action of the series, the two have grown closer after being forced apart. Min-ji now understands more about her father’s past and motivations, and no longer sees him as a timid man who would rather bow than fight. 

In the final episode, they are reunited after Agent Kim fakes his death to escape international accountability for his past acts of espionage. The father and daughter start a new life together under new identities, with the help of the SMD. While they leave the identities of Bank Manager Kim and Kim Min-ji behind, they are somehow still in contact with Han-soo and Jin-cheol, who help the Kims move into their new home.

Will there be a Season 2?

It’s likely—the series has been one of the most successful Korean dramas of the year so far on Netflix and on broadcast television in Korea. According to The Chosun Daily, the production team is currently discussing the possibility of a second season.

If Agent Kim Reactivated does get more episodes, the story will most likely revolve around Agent Kim’s new job at Baekho Employment Agency. In the first season finale, Kim makes a deal with Lee Dong-kyu, a new and enigmatic character who agrees to take down Juhak Construction for our protagonist. The cost is implied to be Agent Kim’s employment at Lee’s mysterious company. 

While we don’t learn much about Lee Dong-kyu in the Netflix series, the character is an important element of the webtoon on which Agent Kim Reactivated is based. In the webtoon, the Baekho Employment Agency, aka the White Tiger Job Center, is a mercenary organization founded and led by Tom Lee. The private company takes on high-risk, high-reward jobs--for the right price. If Agent Kim Reactivated continues for a second season, Agent Kim may find himself in even more dangerous scenarios due to his deal with Lee Dong-kyu.

item.title: Measles Cases in the U.S. Are at a 35-Year High
item.description: New numbers from the CDC reveal a trend that's worrying doctors.

media:content.media:description: The Lubbock Public Health facility on April 9, 2025

item.content:encoded:
Measles is an old scourge that’s rapidly re-emerging as a new one. According to numbers released by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on July 24, there have been 2,318 cases of measles reported nationwide so far in this year, already exceeding the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025. The current figure is the highest incidence of measles in 35 years, a record set back in 1991 when there were 9,643 U.S. cases.

It wasn’t long ago that measles cases were extremely rare in the U.S. In 1963, the first measles vaccine was introduced in the U.S., and decades of steady administration of the shot eventually led to the country being declared measles-free in 2000. There were some scattered infections in the ensuing years—56 cases in 2003, 55 in 2012, 13 in 2020. But this year and last year, the numbers have exploded.

The surge has come amid a backdrop of drastic changes to childhood vaccinations.  In January 2026, the CDC changed the childhood vaccine schedule—despite experts and organizations saying there had been no change in the science—after President Donald Trump directed the agency and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services and a longtime vaccine skeptic, to review how other developed countries issue vaccine recommendations. The new guidelines reduced the number of recommended vaccines for children from 17 to 11. Though the measles vaccine is still on the “recommended” list, recent research published in Science showed that changes in the CDC's vaccine messaging under the Trump Administration reduced the public's trust in the agency and in vaccines, while increasing perceptions that vaccines are not safe.


Even before the second Trump Administration, vaccination rates for measles nationwide were down. Generally, it takes 95% vaccination coverage for a population to achieve what is known as herd immunity, the protection that is afforded when there are so many people inoculated against a disease that the pathogen can’t gain an infectious toehold in a society and reach that small part of the unvaccinated population—generally those who are too young to be vaccinated or those who cannot receive the shots for medical reasons such as compromised immune systems. Vaccination rates are not available for the 2025-2026 school year yet, but for 2024-2025 the number was just 92.5%, down from 95.2% in 2019-2020. 

That much of a drop in vaccination coverage creates pockets for viruses, like the one that causes measles, to spread. Of measles cases so far in 2026 and for the entirety of last year, 93% have been among unvaccinated children, 3% were among children who received just one vaccine dose, and 4% were among kids who received both. This year, 7% of those cases resulted in hospitalizations. There have been no deaths so far this year, but there were three in 2025—one of them an unvaccinated adult, and two of them children with no known underlying health conditions.

“There were two healthy little girls in West Texas that died from measles,” said Dr. Paul Offit, Director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, in an email to TIME. “Those were the first measles deaths in a child in this country in more than 20 years. I think it is fair to say that measles is epidemic in the United States. And if people are coming from outside this country to the United States, they better make sure they’re up-to-date on their immunizations.”

Adds Dr. Peter Hotez, Dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at the Baylor College of Medicine: “For all practical purposes measles has returned to the United States, both in terms of cases and hospitalizations, as well as two needless deaths.  We should expect our annual winter-spring surges of measles to get even worse in subsequent years.  And it won't be just measles—pertussis is also returning, and other childhood infectious diseases might follow."

item.title: Mitch McConnell Shares New Health Update 6 Weeks After Hospitalization
item.description: McConnell revealed earlier this month that he had been hospitalized following a fall, pushing back on speculation of more serious health issues.

media:content.media:description: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) is seen during a Senate Committee on Appropriations, Subcommittee on Department of Defense budget hearing at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., on May 19, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Sen. Mitch McConnell shared a new update on his health on Monday, six weeks after he was initially hospitalized.

In a statement released by his office, the 84-year-old lawmaker said that he was “still working hard to get back to [his] full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky,” and that he was still undergoing “intense physical therapy.” He added that he wouldn’t be able to attend an upcoming event in his home state, called Fancy Farm picnic.

“There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” McConnell said. “As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I’m looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon.”

The statement was accompanied by a message from Congress’ Office of the Attending Physician (OAP), which said that its physicians “visit with the Senator every day, discussing all aspects of his rehabilitation care.”

“Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls,” the office said. “His bout with childhood polio continues to be a significant factor in his mobility. He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

McConnell was hospitalized on June 14. His office initially didn’t share any details of the Republican Senator’s condition, and his ensuing weeks-long absence from the upper chamber with little to no information from his office sparked speculation over McConnell’s health. The growing uncertainty prompted Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, to issue a public letter calling on McConnell to “fully update Kentuckians regarding the current status of [his] health.”

“Over the last several weeks, Kentuckians have grown increasingly concerned about the current state of your health and wellbeing, and ability to hold office in the United States Senate,” Beshear wrote. “As public officeholders, we have made a commitment to our constituents to do our best to represent them and to always be transparent. I believe this requires clear communication about one’s ability to serve.”

Four days later, the Senator revealed that he was hospitalized after a fall. He said that his doctors confirmed that he didn’t break any bones or sustain a concussion, nor did he suffer from any other more serious conditions, such as a heart attack or stroke.

“But,” McConnell said, “I was briefly unconscious and was taken to the hospital. While receiving excellent care over the past several weeks, I’ve also had to deal with a mild case of pneumonia.”

“As much as it frustrates me, this process takes time,” he continued. “And on the advice of my doctors, I won’t be able to return to the Senate floor to vote quite yet. But rest assured that, in the meantime, I’m not taking a break from the Senate business that matters to you.”

He went on to say that part of the reason he decided that he would retire in January, when his term comes to an end, “was being honest about the demands of Senate work.”

The Kentucky Senator has had several health scares before this one, including multiple falls in recent years

item.title: Why Tensions Are Mounting Between Trump and Republican Senate Leader Thune
item.description: A long-simmering conflict between President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune is breaking out into the open as the upper chamber approaches its August recess.

media:content.media:description: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) (L) and President Donald Trump arrive at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on June 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C.

item.content:encoded:
A long-simmering conflict between President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune is breaking out into the open as the upper chamber approaches its August recess without making progress on a restrictive voting bill the President has underlined as his top legislative priority.

Trump reiterated his festering frustrations with Thune on Monday.

“John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to ‘leave town’ until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER, where Republicans can then quickly pass everything they ever dreamed of, including a full and deep throated SAVE AMERICA ACT, the Budget, and the ever looming Debt Ceiling disaster, 1929!” Trump said in a Truth Social post. 

“The Dumocrats will do it on day one, and can’t believe how lucky they got with this Senate leadership,” he continued. “Remember, stupidity always brings LOSING & DEATH!”

Tensions have been mounting between the President and the Republican Senate leader for months over the stalled SAVE America Act, a contentious piece of legislation that would impose stricter voter identification requirements around the country. Trump has aggressively promoted the bill, even vowing not to sign any other bills into law until Congress passes it. But forward momentum on the bill, which passed the House in February, has come to a halt in the upper chamber, where Thune said that Republicans don’t have enough votes to pass it.

Trump has repeatedly encouraged Senate Republicans to end the filibuster, which gives the minority party the ability to delay or block legislation by dragging out debate, effectively requiring a 60-vote threshold for most bills to pass the upper chamber. But many Republican lawmakers have objected to the idea of ending the filibuster—including Thune, who previously said it would be a “bad idea” and that the filibuster “has protected this country.”

The Senate Majority Leader has also indicated that Republicans in the upper chamber don’t have the votes to pass another measure Trump has pushed, a $95 billion budget proposal that would help fund the President’s war in Iran and other White House priorities.

“As I’ve said before, you got to get to 50, and I can’t count to 50 right now on a budget resolution,” Thune told reporters last week.

The situation has provoked the President’s ire—and, now that the Senate is set to go on recess at the end of next week, Trump has been renewing his pressure on Thune. Last week, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said that the President wants to have “as much of the SAVE America (Act) passed as possible” before senators go on recess.

“His patience is running out,” she said during the White House press briefing on Thursday.

The day before, Trump slammed the Senate during a rally in Georgia, calling the upper chamber “a place that you send things when you want them to die.”

“Everybody call John Thune,” Trump continued. “He’s the leader of the Republican party, and tell him to get this stuff approved.”

Thune fired back at the White House on Thursday: “Maybe she,” he said, referring to Leavitt, “or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes.”

“Instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats," Thune told reporters. “And if there are Republicans that they think are gettable, get on the phone. Let’s get them to ‘yes.’”

item.title: The U.S. Is Now At Its Worst Level of Wildfire Preparedness. What Does That Mean?
item.description: Here's what that means.

media:content.media:description: A view of burning area as crews battle with wildfire named as 'Mines Fire' in Santa Clara County, Calif. on July 26, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Federal officials have moved the national wildfire preparedness level to its highest level: a five out of five. That means that, as we approach peak fire season in the U.S., federal agencies might not have enough resources to address every new fire. 

What are U.S. wildfire preparedness levels?

A number of federal agencies, including the U.S. Forest Service, U.S. Fire Administration, and the National Weather Service, are responsible for allocating federal resources for tackling wildfires, like helicopters, airtankers, funding, or firefighters. The wildfire preparedness levels, which range from the lowest, 1, to the highest, 5, help the agencies track what resources are available. “It’s a framework for determining resource allocation,” says Craig Clements, director of the Wildfire Interdisciplinary Research Center at San Jose State University. “As the fire season progresses, those resources are used around the country by different agencies. When we get to level five, that means that resources are running low because there's so many incidents ongoing.”

What does a national preparedness level 5 mean for wildfire risk?

At level 5, national resources are already committed to fighting fires around the country. “The fire hazard is at its greatest, and the resources are at their most strained level,” says Peter Sunderland, professor of fire protection engineering at the University of Maryland. 

That means that federal agencies might not have the resources to respond to new fires. “If there are existing fires, they won't pull anybody off those fires,” says Sunderland. “But as new fires arise, the state managers can't expect the same level of service that they'd get at level one through four. In other words, they may say we just can't help with that new fire.”

That presents a new challenge, since fires are easier to put out in the first few hours after they start, a period of time known as the “initial attack.” “[Firefighters] try to get helicopters and crews on as soon as possible, so that way it doesn't become a big fire,” Sunderland says. “Once it becomes bigger and larger, it takes a lot more resources to contain that fire, and it takes a lot more time.” 

Wildfire season in the U.S. usually lasts from May to November, peaking in the summer. It’s not uncommon for the U.S. to reach level 5 in July. “This is pretty typical,” Clements notes. “It’s almost August, so we are in the prime time of fire season.” The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) previously declared a level 5 preparedness level in July of 2018, 2021, and 2024. 

Does wildfire preparedness level 5 affect me if I don't live near a fire?

If you don’t live near an area at risk, you might not be directly impacted by a fire. However, as wildfires in Canada earlier this summer proved, smoke can travel a long distance from the initial blaze, impacting air quality for people thousands of miles away. 

Why is this year such a dangerous wildfire year?

Much of the country has seen dry, hot conditions this year, setting the stage for an active wildfire season. This past winter was the second-warmest in U.S. history, with 19 states—including Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Texas—all experiencing one of their 10 driest winters on record, according to NOAA.

This year has already set a record for the number of fires. So far in 2026, the U.S. has seen 41,779 fires—the most one season has seen in the last 10 years. 

How long does wildfire season last and how is climate change impacting wildfires?


“We are seeing more and more climate extremes,” says Sunderland. “Generally we're having drier summers and higher winds.” That creates the perfect conditions for wildfires to spread.

Fire season is also lasting longer than in decades past thanks to climate change. While wildfire season might once have lasted around four months, they can now stretch on for six to eight months in some areas. 

The fires we see now are also more severe than those of a decade ago—in no small part due to climate change. A recent study led by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles found that forest fires now burn 10 times as much acreage annually as in 1985, while high-severity fires alone increased thirtyfold in California between 1985 and 2024.

What should you do if your area is under high fire danger?

If you live in a fire-prone area, make sure you know your evacuation plan well before you need it. Listen to authorities and evacuate while it is still safe to do so. There are steps you can take to protect your home ahead of time—like clearing out brush, clearing your gutters, and staying up to date on fire code. Nearly nine in 10 wildfires are human caused, so be vigilant about accidental fires when camping outside, says Clements: “As long as we can limit the amount of ignitions, we can get out of this problem.”

item.title: What We Know About the Seattle Food Festival Shooting
item.description: One suspect is in custody and another remains at large following the Sunday shooting, which left three people dead and four others wounded.

media:content.media:description: Police officers walk on patrol at the scene of a mass shooting at the Bite of Seattle food festival in Seattle, Washington, on July 26, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
One suspect is in custody and a second remains at large after a shooting at a food festival in Seattle on Sunday evening left three people dead and four others wounded, according to police. 

The shooting took place near Seattle’s Space Needle at Bite of Seattle, an annual food festival that draws more than 350,000 people, according to its website. 

The victims and suspects have not yet been publicly identified. A search continued for the second suspect on Monday. Assistant Police Chief Tyrone Davis said at a press conference following the shooting on Sunday that there is “no outstanding threat to the community.”

“What happened here today at the Seattle Center was an unbelievable tragedy, a horrific act of violence,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said. “My heart right now is with the victims and their families, and with everyone in our community who is reeling from what happened here today.”

Here’s what we know about the shooting so far. 

What happened? 

Authorities on Sunday began responding to reports of a shooting at the Seattle Center, a public arts and entertainment area north of downtown Seattle, around 6 p.m. local time. 

Two of the people killed in the shooting died at the scene. Four others were injured, including a toddler, and taken to Harborview Medical Center to be treated for their injuries. One patient who was taken into surgery in critical condition later died as a result of her injuries, police announced late Sunday.

Investigators believe the two suspects in the incident were shooting at each other, Police Chief Shon Barnes said at a Monday press conference. One suspect surrendered to police at the scene, while the other fled. Wilson on Monday said that “no police weapons were discharged” at the scene. 

“Our officers were there within seconds,” Davis said on Sunday. “They performed emergency aid to the wounded until the Seattle Fire Department was on scene. Simultaneously, officers launched a search for the people responsible for this senseless violence.” 

Police also recovered two firearms at the scene. Wilson said Monday that camera footage from the Seattle Center is in the process of being recovered. 

As of Monday morning, police have not publicly discussed a potential motive for the shooting.

“I don't know if it's gang activity, but certainly group activity,” Barnes said on Monday when asked if the shooting was gang-related. “We have small groups that appear to be at odds with each other, and in our city, 0.01% of the population is connected to 52 percent of our shootings, most of which are young people.”

Who are the victims?

The names of the victims have not been made public. Wilson on Monday said that their official identification will come from the King County Medical Examiner's Office.

The Seattle Police Department (SPD) described the deceased as a 19-year-old man, a 44-year-old man, and a 56-year-old woman. 

One of the four wounded victims was a 2-year-old boy, according to police. The others were adults.

All four “remained in stable condition at local hospitals” as of Monday morning, the department said in a news release shortly after 1 a.m. Officials noted later Monday that the two-year-old was in “satisfactory condition” at Harborview Medical Center. 

Who are the suspects?

Little information has so far been released about the person in custody, or the suspect still at large. Wilson said at the press conference on Monday that the detained individual was a “a 15-year-old juvenile in connection with the shooting.” 

He was set to make his first appearance in a court hearing Monday afternoon, she added. 

Davis said “there may be more” suspects, stating that "we're still trying to figure this out.” He encouraged people who were at the scene to come forward and help the department locate other potential suspects.

“There are witnesses. They're not coming forward,” he said. “We need people to be brave, to reach out to us. You can do so anonymously. We know that we have people who probably have evidence or have information that they can share with us.”

Barnes said that “it is possible” when asked if one of the deceased victims was Sunday’s suspected second shooter. “But we do not know that that is the case until we do the investigation,” he said. 

What officials are saying

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal, whose district includes Seattle Center and who attended Sunday’s press conference, said that she was “absolutely horrified” by the shooting. She added that Seattle was “coordinating across all levels of government,” when asked about the federal government’s knowledge of the shooting.

“My heart goes out to the victims, their families, and our whole Seattle community,” Jayapal said on X. 

Wilson commented on the high incidence of gun violence in the U.S. after the shooting. 

“We have far too much gun violence in this city and in this country, and we’re coming off of a week in Seattle where we’ve had three major incidents of gun violence in just a few days,” she said. 

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said at the news conference that “our hearts go out to everybody who’s impacted by this.” 

“I can’t imagine being the parent of a two-year-old toddler, for example, who’s injured in a shooting like this,” he said.

 

The state’s Sens. Maria Cantwell and Patty Murray also expressed their condolences to the victims and gratitude to authorities.

item.title: Republican Lawmaker Breaks Ranks With Trump Over U.S.-Saudi Arabia Nuclear Deal
item.description: “We're bombing a country to keep them from getting a nuclear weapon, but we're signing a deal with another country,” said the Republican Senator.

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump (C), alongside (L/R) Sen. Mike Lee, Sen. Rick Scott, Sen. John Barrasso, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune after a lunch meeting with Senate Republicans at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 24, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s civil nuclear deal with ‌Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among not only Democratic lawmakers, but also within the GOP.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana raised issue with Trump’s proposed arrangement, firmly answering “no” when asked if he was comfortable with it, insisting it’s “just not good timing.”

“Maybe someday, but not right now,” Kennedy told Face the Nation on Sunday, pointing to the resumed Iran war as a key point of his opposition.

“We're bombing a country to keep them from getting a nuclear weapon, but we're signing a deal with another country,” he said. “I know it's a commercial agreement, but that the world perceives, as possibly, someday, leading to a nuclear weapon.”

Kennedy referred to the moment as a “hair trigger,” pointing to the conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East, and America’s strained relationship with Europe as examples of the tense political climate that has left people “scared.”

The U.S. and Saudi Arabia announced they had reached a civil nuclear agreement on Wednesday, in addition to signing an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement.

The U.S. Department of Energy described the deal as “a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” that “provides great access for American companies in the Saudi nuclear energy program, benefiting American industry, workers, and supply chains while helping to meet Saudi energy needs.”

However, the day after the agreement was signed, Trump added a condition—stating the deal is dependent on Riyadh recognizing Israel under the Abraham Accords.

“The civil nuclear deal (there will be no enrichment of material) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” Trump declared via Truth Social.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump reaffirmed his stance and told reporters that he had not spoken about the accords with U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright before the cabinet member signed the deal with Saudi Minister of Energy His Royal Highness (HRH) Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

“We didn’t talk about it, but it was always understood, and Chris knew and Saudi Arabia knew, that if they didn’t join the Abraham Accords… I’m not going to do the deal,” Trump said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu showed support for the idea, saying “Saudi Arabia's joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.”

Trump’s demand for Saudi Arabia to recognize Israel placed further doubt on the deal for some, including Sen. Kennedy.

“I don't think it's going to happen, anyway, because the President's conditioned it on Saudi Arabia recognizing Israel, and they're not, they're not going to do that,” he said.

Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the add-on condition to the deal, but Riyadh officials have long maintained they would not recognize Israel without a clear pathway toward a Palestinian state.

The post-signing condition has also prompted a response from Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who called it a “complete whiplash.”

“The Saudis have been very clear that they will normalize relations with Israel when we’re on a clear path toward developing a Palestinian state, living side-by-side—security for both Palestinians and Israelis,” Van Hollen told This Week. “That has been the Saudi position. And so, what the Trump Administration did was a bait-and-switch scheme.”

What happens now?

The U.S.-Saudi Arabia civil nuclear deal—commonly known as a 123 agreement—needs to be transmitted to Congress for approval.

Congress has 90 days to review and, if desired, raise votes to object to the deal. If Congress does not pass a resolution to block the deal, it goes into force.

There would need to be a two-thirds majority to override a presidential veto. As lawmakers across party aisles have raised concerns and questions about the deal, the road ahead is uncertain.

item.title: 15 Habits Infectious Disease Experts Swear By to Avoid Getting Sick
item.description: They follow surprisingly simple rules to prevent illness.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Daniel Griffin doesn’t like to get sick. The first reason why is obvious—the congestion, the aching, the cough that overstays its welcome, the unpleasant stomach symptoms.

The second is a matter of professional dignity. "It's almost like a gardener with dead plants," says Griffin, chief of the division of infectious disease at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y. and president of Parasites Without Borders. "I really don't want to be sick—because then the infectious disease doctor got sick.”

So what do infectious disease doctors and experts like him do differently than the rest of us when it comes to preventing illness? Not as much as you'd think. Infectious disease specialists aren't disinfecting every surface or hiding from the outside world. Instead, they've built a collection of practical habits into their daily lives—simple routines that reduce risk without making life less enjoyable.

We asked six infectious disease experts which habits they never skip.

Set up your kitchen so cross-contamination can't happen

Jill Roberts tries to take the guesswork out of food safety. "One of the major causes of foodborne illness is cross-contamination," says Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. "It's when you have something that's raw and you get microbes from the raw thing into the ready-to-eat thing." 

Her favorite solution: color-coded cutting boards. Meat always goes on the red one; vegetables never do. "If your meat is always on the red cutting board, you're never gonna have your salad stuff on your red cutting board,” she says. 

Order matters just as much. She makes the salad first, puts it in the refrigerator, and only then brings out the red boards and raw meat. Once she starts handling meat, she’s vigilant about sanitizing any surfaces she may have contaminated—from the counters and sink to the faucet handles and refrigerator door.

Wash your produce under running water—not in a bowl

Some people think rinsing produce means filling a bowl with water and letting everything soak. But that's not the best approach. "What you actually need is that little bit of friction to break the surface," says Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant professor of clinical medicine at Weill Cornell Medical College. About 30 seconds under running water, while gently rubbing the produce with your hands, does far more than a passive soak.

The problem with a bowl is that you're washing everything in the same water. "If you have one piece that's contaminated, that water could contaminate the other vegetables," Torres says. Running water washes germs away instead of moving them from one piece of produce to another. It won't remove everything—Cyclospora, for example, doesn't simply rinse off—but it does reduce bacteria, viruses, and even some pesticide residue. 

Microwave your kitchen sponge

A sponge is a nearly perfect habitat for germs: damp, warm, and studded with food particles, sitting next to the counter where you just set down raw chicken. "Sponges and wet dishcloths are really good at growing bacteria," says Kelley Steury, a clinical associate professor in the school of public health at the University of Nevada, Reno, who specializes in veterinary preventive medicine. Her routine: Rinse her sponge until no food particles come out, then microwave it for 20 seconds. Just make sure it's wet. "If you did it when it was pretty dry, you could start a fire,” she says.

Brush your teeth like it's infection control

Most people brush their teeth to prevent cavities. Torres brushes hers to prevent infections.

"At least 25% of infections that I see are related to dental disease," she says. Here's why: Every day, small amounts of bacteria slip into your bloodstream, and a healthy immune system clears them without you ever noticing. Cavities and gum disease change the equation. They allow more bacteria—and more aggressive bacteria—to leak into the blood, which Torres describes as "a highway to all your organs." In some cases, she says, doctors can trace an infection back to the mouth because the bacteria involved simply don't live anywhere else.

That makes brushing about much more than fresh breath. "Rinsing alone wouldn’t replace it, because you really need that mechanical brushing to break down that film of bacteria," Torres says. Hospitals have even started treating basic oral care as a form of infection prevention, she says—which is a pretty compelling reason to take it seriously at home, too.

Rethink the rug in your bathroom

Your bath mat outside the tub should be washable, hung to dry between uses, and tossed in the laundry about once a week. "We don't leave the wet stuff on the floor, because that's gross," Roberts says. A damp bath mat can also spread athlete's foot from one person to another.

As for the old-fashioned rug wrapped around the base of the toilet? Roberts would get rid of it altogether. Rubber backings don’t often hold up well in the wash, which means it probably doesn't get cleaned as thoroughly as it should. "Especially if you have kids, they don't aim well," she says. "You have splash-overs." In other words: Nothing around the toilet should be soaking anything up.

Leave your shoes at the door

Shoes pick up a lot more than dirt. Every sidewalk has been shared with other people, their pets, and whatever else has passed through. Dr. Cesar J. Figueroa Ortiz, an infectious diseases specialist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, would rather not track any of that across the floors where his family walks and spends time—so shoes come off at the door.

His job reinforces the habit. Hospitals are meticulously cleaned, but there's always "the risk of bringing pathogens with you on your shoes," he says. 

Open a window before company comes over

Before guests arrive, most people wipe down the counters. Chin-Hong thinks they should be paying more attention to the air. "I respect air more than surfaces," he says. "You're probably going to have a bigger bang for your buck when you think about ventilation."

His solution is simple: crack a window. If the air conditioning is running, make sure it's bringing in fresh outdoor air rather than recirculating the same indoor air all evening, he adds.

Wash your hands like you're not in a hurry

Even infectious disease doctors don't always practice perfect hand hygiene. Griffin has watched colleagues race out of a public restroom because they were about to miss a lecture at a conference. "They're so anxious to get back out because they're missing whatever the lecture is, and they're not really doing proper hand hygiene," he says. "Even the people that should know better are rushing back out."

And when people do wash their hands, they're often rushing through that, too. "Nobody's singing 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' to time themselves," Griffin says (besides him).

His other rule is knowing when soap and water beat sanitizer. (Basically always.) Alcohol-based hand sanitizer doesn't kill everything: Norovirus—the highly contagious stomach bug behind many cruise ship outbreaks—is particularly resistant. Soap and water keep you safe, though, so if someone around you is vomiting or has diarrhea, Griffin says, head for the sink.

Use your shirt tail

Steury will happily look a little strange to save herself a bout with a germ. "Someone might look at me and think I'm crazy, but I'll use the bottom of a shirt, like my shirt tails," she says—or the hem of a cardigan, whatever's handy—around her hand when she has to touch certain surfaces.

She's selective about when she does it. What worries her are high-touch surfaces that are indoors and out of the sun: elevator buttons, soda fountain dispensers, and the door handle to a medical clinic, for instance. And if she does touch one of those surfaces directly, she waits until she can wash her hands before touching her eyes, nose, or mouth. 

Decline the grocery-store sample

Before you accept that free cube of cheese, think about the cart you're pushing.

"I always think about what happened to the grocery cart before you got there," Roberts says. "Somebody picked up raw chicken. Somebody picked up raw seafood. And all of that is on the cart. It's on the handle."

Then someone offers you a toothpick with a sample. "I'm supposed to take my hand off this dirty cart and then take that food and put it in my mouth?" she says. "There's no way."

Wear sandals in every locker-room shower

At the gym, Torres worries less about the person coughing on the treadmill than the surfaces her bare skin touches. Benches, mats, and other shared equipment can harbor MRSA and fungi like ringworm—even at the nicest gyms. She wipes equipment down before using it, not just afterward, and if there aren't disinfecting wipes available, she puts a towel between herself and the bench.

The locker-room shower gets its own rule. "It's this wet, damp floor, walking around the locker room, walking around the joint showers," she says. "I always recommend bringing a pair of sandals." Foot fungus is the biggest concern, and some infections can be surprisingly difficult to get rid of.

Wash any cuts before reaching for the antiseptic

Most of us instinctively reach for the antiseptic after nicking a finger. Chin-Hong heads for the sink instead. "The more important thing is to rinse it well with running water and soap, which is more important than the aggressive disinfectant," he says. Disinfectants don't kill everything, but running water can physically flush away germs before they have a chance to cause trouble.

His reasoning comes down to one simple idea. "Running things are better than stagnant things," Chin-Hong says. "We get infections when things are in stasis rather than in movement." It's the same reason standing water becomes a mosquito breeding ground. 

Pack a pair of tweezers

Torres never leaves for a weekend in tick country without packing a pair of tweezers. It might sound excessive, she admits, but after years of treating tickborne illnesses, it's become second nature. "This is a little unusual—maybe my colleagues don't do this," she says, "but whenever I go away for a weekend, I always pack a pair of tweezers."

These days, that means much of the country: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South, and parts of the West Coast. After spending time in tall grass or wooded areas, do a full-body tick check, paying special attention to places they like to hide, like under the arms and behind the knees. 

It matters more than you might think. "Most people that develop Lyme disease or tickborne illness have no recollection of ever being bitten by a tick or ever seeing a tick," Torres says. She's also vigilant against ticks to try to prevent alpha-gal syndrome—the tick-triggered allergy to red meat that has become increasingly common.

Reapply bug spray like it's sunscreen

Bug spray is a permanent fixture in Chin-Hong's travel bag. "I respect mosquitoes," he says. "They actually kill more people than any other animal." It's West Nile season, and dengue keeps extending its reach into new parts of the U.S., so he travels with insect repellent as a matter of course.

The biggest mistake people make, he says, is treating bug spray like a one-and-done product. "It's like sunscreen. You don't get away with just applying it once." If you're outdoors all day, reapply at least every six hours. He also recommends choosing a repellent with about 20% to 50% DEET—or 20% picaridin if you prefer to avoid DEET—and remembering that the mosquitoes most likely to spread disease are busiest from dusk to dawn.

Rinse your toothbrush with bottled water when traveling abroad

Most travelers remember to avoid the tap water in destinations with questionable water supplies. Griffin worries about the toothbrush. "We tell people to be careful of ice cubes and tap water and all the rest," he says. "But then people brush their teeth with the tap water."

He calls what often follows "third-day sickness." By then, your toothbrush has been rinsed repeatedly in tap water and left to sit in a warm, humid bathroom—giving any lingering microbes plenty of time to multiply before the brush goes right back into your mouth. His solution takes just a few seconds: rinse your mouth and toothbrush with bottled water, too.

item.title: ICE Reportedly Set to Ramp Up Operations Against Haitian Migrants After TPS Ruling
item.description: The potential crackdown follows a Supreme Court ruling that allowed the Trump Administration to end Haitians’ Temporary Protected Status.

media:content.media:description: Haitian flags are displayed on a store in the Little Haiti neighborhood of the Brooklyn borough in New York City on June 25, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
More than 300,000 Haitian immigrants are set to lose their ability to legally live and work in the U.S. on Monday, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly preparing to escalate its operations to arrest and deport some of them.

Those expanded operations could start as early as this week, according to reports from Fox News and CBS News, which cite unnamed federal sources. Ohio will reportedly be heavily targeted, particularly Springfield, where President Donald Trump had, in 2024, falsely accused Haitian migrants of eating residents’ pets.

A potential crackdown on Haitian migrants follows the Supreme Court’s June ruling that allowed the Trump Administration, for the time being, to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for those fleeing violence and natural disaster in Haiti and Syria. The binding mandate of that ruling is expected to be transmitted to lower courts on Monday.

It remains unclear how aggressive the reported ICE campaign will be, and if Haiti can successfully reintegrate an influx of returnees. But Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, director-general of Haiti’s National Office of Migration, told local media earlier this month that following a conversation with the U.S. embassy in the country, Haitians should expect weekly deportation flights carrying about 250 former TPS status grantees.

The court ruling and its expected implementation have stirred anxiety among Haitians in the U.S. who could lose their livelihoods and may be sent back to the crisis-stricken Caribbean nation. It could also have a profound impact on the U.S. economy. A January 2026 fact sheet from immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates that about 200,000 Haitian TPS holders are in the U.S. workforce, including 15,000 agricultural workers, 13,000 nursing assistants, and thousands of others in various industries.

In a statement to CBS News, DHS said it “does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” adding: “What we would say now is it’s closing time which means you don't have to go home, but you can't stay here… The good news is it's not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home.”

Conditions in Haiti still severe

During his first-term Administration, Trump targeted TPS, a program since 1990 that has allowed migrants from designated countries with unsafe conditions—such as armed conflict, natural disaster, epidemics, or other extraordinary conditions—to reside and work legally in the U.S.

In his second-term Administration, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved to terminate TPS designations for several countries, including Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Yemen. In many announcements ending those protections, then-Secretary Kristi Noem emphasized that TPS was designed to be temporary, and she argued that the living conditions in many of the countries with TPS designation have improved. Any extension to the TPS designations for those countries, the department said, would be “contrary” to the “national interest.”

Persons who lose their TPS status must find another lawful basis for staying in the U.S. or depart the U.S.; otherwise they may be removed. 

But these TPS rescissions and terminations have been legally challenged. In February, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Administration’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation, though the Trump Administration appealed, eventually leading to the Supreme Court ruling.

Haiti first received a TPS designation in 2010 after a magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck the country in January that year, leaving more than 300,000 people dead and displacing over a million others. Since then, the country has been a TPS designee: the first-term Trump Administration’s planned termination was delayed mainly due to court injunctions and other rulings, and the succeeding Biden Administration renewed and extended those designations.

As DHS Secretary, Noem reviewed Haiti’s TPS designation and her department found that there were no “extraordinary and temporary conditions” that prevented Haitian nationals from returning safely, and that even if there were, allowing them to stay longer in the U.S. went against national interest.

The State Department, however, notes that conditions in the country are not that safe: as of July 10, it holds the highest-level travel warning to Americans, urging them not to visit. A state of national emergency has been in effect since 2024 because of gang-linked criminality and violence: an estimated 26 gangs, at times heavily armed, control 90% of the capital Port-au-Prince and its surrounding areas, and the nation’s government has had a hard time putting the situation under control. 

According to the latest report by the International Organization for Migration, the violence in Haiti has displaced nearly 1.5 million persons, of whom more than half are women and girls.

‘A huge mistake’

Some Republicans have opposed the Trump Administration’s plan to end the TPS designation for Haiti. 

In April, the GOP-controlled House passed legislation that would require the Homeland Security Secretary to redesignate Haiti to TPS until a few months into 2029, with 10 Republicans siding with Democrats. The legislation is now pending in the Senate, where the latest attempt to pass it was blocked on July 22 by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R, Mo.). But even if the bill passes both chambers, the White House earlier said that the President’s advisers would recommend vetoing it.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R, Fla.) told CBS News earlier this month that while Haiti is a “failed state,” he thinks “deporting Haitians that are under TPS right now, back to Haiti, would be a huge mistake.”

Markwayne Mullin, who took over for Noem as DHS Secretary in March, defended the decision to end Haiti’s TPS designation. Speaking to CNN in June, Mullin said that those staying in the U.S. under TPS have “had plenty of time” to explore other options to legally stay in the U.S. long-term, instead of banking solely on what was intended to be a temporary measure.

Asked about whether Haiti qualified as “safe,” Mullin told CNN that such a qualification “isn’t quite just that simple,” and he argued that the State Department travel advisory had Americans in mind and not Haitians. 

“There isn’t a more generous country in the world than the United States,” Mullin said of the TPS designation, “but we don’t want people to take advantage of it.”

item.title: Hulu’s Riveting Revenge Thriller Furious Is Going to Haunt You
item.description: Hulu's riveting revenge thriller interrogates the psychology of victimhood and the myth that the justice system protects the vulnerable.

media:content.media:description: Emmy Rossum, left, and Quincy Tyler Bernstine in Furious

item.content:encoded:
Midway through the Hulu thriller series Furious, it’s the middle of the night and two female FBI agents are on their way to investigate a lead when one notices the other’s bruises. “Who did that to your face?” demands Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), who leads some of the Bureau’s most horrific sex crimes cases, as she pours liquor into her coffee cup. When Alice (Emmy Rossum), a rookie agent who worked as a Brooklyn homicide detective until her abusive, alcoholic cop boyfriend (Jake Lacy) ruined her police career, confesses that she met a man on the internet and asked him to hit her, she’s surprised to find her superior unfazed. “You think I’ve never let someone take a few whacks at this piñata?” Nora cracks. They both cackle. 

If you find yourself laughing along with them—or can, at least, imagine why two women who have chosen to professionally immerse themselves in nightmarish sexual violence might seek a consensual version of it and also find the humor in that proclivity—then it’s likely you’ll be able to get on Furious’ wavelength. Created by Elizabeth Meriwether (Dying for Sex, New Girl) and premiering, with three episodes, on July 27, the series is more straightforward in its plot than the typical convoluted crime thriller but also more complex in its layered, often contradictory ideas. Its cat-and-mouse setup resembles that of Killing Eve: a troubled, underestimated female agent chases an eccentric, possibly psychopathic female killer. As its title suggests, one of its subjects is women’s rage. Yet, at its core, Furious is a haunting interrogation of the psychology of victimhood, the logic of revenge, and the myth that the justice system exists to protect the vulnerable, and its conclusions are too messy to resolve into a pat fable of empowerment or healing.

Although stickier questions of guilt and accountability arise, Meriwether doesn’t waste time on an initial murder mystery. Only after we watch a girlish woman in a cat mask (Say Nothing’s Lola Petticrew) administer a lethal injection to an incapacitated man, in between fetching candy for Brooklyn trick-or-treaters, do we meet the agent who will soon be on her trail. Having entered FBI training after her domestic violence allegations against Lacy’s Marshall made her a pariah at the precinct, Alice is pulled off desk duty at the Bureau to help investigate the Halloween murder. Behind that request is Dan (Scoot McNairy), the only NYPD detective still speaking to her and someone with whom she has quite a bit of history. (There aren’t many uncomplicated relationships in this show.) When the ad-hoc partners notice telling similarities between their new case—whose victim is the son of a billionaire, and whose female suspect has yet to be identified—and a year-old unsolved murder, Alice develops a theory that the two targets were involved in a child sex-trafficking ring and that their killer was one of the girls they trafficked.

She’s right, though that doesn’t make her investigation any easier. The murderer, whose name is Catherine but who goes by many other aliases, has a one-track mind set to revenge. Moving between domestic violence shelters and subsistence scams, she manipulates kindhearted nonprofit workers, nepo babies who fetishize her sex-worker past, and people who fall closer to the middle of the good-evil spectrum—whatever it takes to keep crossing names off her hit list. The collateral damage of Catherine’s quest can be devastating. Yet it’s hard to hate her. She’s clearly not a sociopath. She cares about children and is capable of authentic tenderness even when it serves no strategic purpose; when she harms innocent people, it palpably hurts her.

Just as Catherine is willing to inflict pain in the service of vengeance, Nora has resigned herself to absorbing it in the potentially fruitless service of justice. When Alice, who had previously asked to be assigned to Nora’s team, seeks her help on the case, the weary agent is locked in her office reviewing child sexual assault materials. “Why do you want to work in the basement on sex crimes and crimes against children?” Nora asks Alice. “Do you hate yourself? Don’t answer that.” By the time she playfully compares their heads to piñatas, we know that both women would, at least on some days, respond in the affirmative. 

Nora harbors no illusions of heroism, which might explain why she drinks so much. Toward the end of the premiere, she dissects Medusa’s origin story for Alice, explaining that the mythical hag’s snakey mane was a punishment—imposed by Athena, no less—for the crime of being raped by Poseidon. “She’s a victim,” Nora says. “But it doesn’t make her a good person. It turns her into a monster.” Like Catherine. “Juries want to believe that women who are victims of violence,” she continues, “but in my experience being a victim of violence just makes you colder, more calculating. Victims of violence are the most violent.” Also? Justice is an impossible fantasy. “Anything you do, the ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never.”

Speeches like this often come at the end of today's bleaker crime dramas—”Forget it, Jake. It’s Chinatown,” but for viewers so distracted or dense, they need dialogue that spells out why Chinatown is a lost cause. Meriwether, whose best work interprets the motivations of apparently incomprehensible women like The Dropout’s Elizabeth Holmes and, in Dying for Sex, the real terminal cancer patient turned sexual explorer Molly Kochan, is doing something different. By placing Nora’s monologue so early in the series, then sending her all the way down the rabbit hole with Alice anyway, Furious is showing us a very smart person who has consciously committed to a lost cause. It’s also warning us against expecting the satisfying resolution, with villains punished and institutions redeemed, that draws so many people to detective stories. 

In the seven episodes that follow, Meriwether piles on complications and thematic filters. There are parallels to the Epstein saga; tensions between an insular, blue-collar police force and federal agents with elite educations; systemic corruption; office politics. Bitter irony abounds, as when Nora, who is Black, attends a workplace mental health seminar in which a white, male supervisor who once mistreated her pretends to care about employees’ trauma. “What about anger?” she asks. Gender and race aren’t the only vectors of oppression the show considers. While wealth disparity plays pretty much exactly the role you’d expect, nuanced depictions of disability—particularly by Ramy actor Steve Way—challenge easy assumptions about personal agency in ways that relate to but are never conflated with the multiple abuse storylines.

As Nora’s speech and Catherine’s kind moments suggest, characters’ actions don’t consistently reflect their overall moral stance, which is often based on misunderstandings and falsehoods, its validity unknowable even to them. Being a woman, a survivor, or a person with physical differences doesn’t make a person righteous. Everyone you might consider a hero of this story will, at some point, do something abhorrent. “We become evil to fight evil,” says Nora, but if the most pernicious evildoers of all are uncatchable, how can the ends justify the means? Oscar contenders like Promising Young Woman and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri have also asked whether revenge, specifically as a response to sexual violence, can rebalance the moral universe, or if it’s ultimately suicidal. But both movies were glib thought experiments that distanced us from their characters to argue their points. Furious takes advantage of its longer runtime to get close to these people in pain. It never reduces them to cartoons.  

At the very center of its tangle of experiences and identities, objectives and conflicts, is Alice. She, Catherine, and Nora are all mirrors for one another, similarly obsessed with righting wrongs and punishing abusers of people and power as they are. (All three performances are Emmy-worthy, but my favorite is Bernstine’s. The Tony nominee and Power franchise alum brings the right mix of humor and defiance to animate a character who might otherwise come off as just a hypocritical sad sack.) Nora and Catherine have committed to opposite paths. But Alice doesn’t know what she wants—the pursuit of justice through legally prescribed channels or bloody revenge exacted by any means necessary. What is she even doing in this investigation, chasing a serial killer or trying to bring down a sex-trafficking ring? Putting Catherine in prison or helping her vanquish the men who hurt her? Does she want Marshall to apologize or change or be punished or fired or die? Why is she voluntarily taking on work that reopens her old wounds when she could start healing them with a decent man and a safe desk job? For Furious, there are no right answers. And if there were, they would be no match for the demands anger makes.

item.title: 6 Easy Ways to Move More While Working from Home
item.description: Even a little activity during the remote workday can help you focus, improve your mood and energy levels, and relieve stress.
item.content:encoded:
At most desk jobs, you’ll be sitting down for the majority of the day. But remote work creates a particularly sedentary environment. There’s no need to walk from your front door to the car or train station. There are no aisles of cubicles to maneuver on your bathroom break or colleagues to stand around with at the water cooler. “We're just sitting there in front of the screen by ourselves,” says Mary Jayne Rogers, an exercise physiologist based in Albuquerque, who’s on the certification advisory board of the American Council on Exercise. 

This immobility has real downsides. “Prolonged sitting can increase the risk of heart disease and high blood pressure, even if you're otherwise active,” says Amy Bantham, past president of the Physical Activity Alliance. It also makes our fascia—the connective tissue that supports every structure, from our muscles and bones to our nerves and organs—stiffen up, causing ripple effects throughout the body that can impact our heart, lungs, gut, and even our brain, she says. 

While giving yourself some adult recess during the work day might seem indulgent, it can actually make you more productive. Even a little activity can help you focus, improve your mood and energy levels, and relieve stress. “You will feel better almost immediately,” Bantham says. 

Fortunately, remote work means there’s no one around to give you side-eye for doing jumping jacks between emails. Here are a few simple ways to move more when you’re working from home. 

Create your own commute

During the time you’d otherwise spend commuting, Bantham suggests taking a walk. She runs her own consulting business from home and likes to go for a stroll and call a friend before work. Similarly, Lindsey Bomgren, a personal trainer based in Minneapolis, gets in her steps each morning while using her phone’s talk-to-text app to draft emails and write herself notes. “I can start my day out walking, wrapping my head around my to-do list,” she says. 

Then, at the end of the day, Bomgren makes a point to do active errands around the house before her kids get home. “I’ll run up and down the stairs three times just to get laundry in, clean up, set out stuff for dinner,” she says. This gets her moving and helps her transition from work mode to mom mode.

Find ways to move while you work

Over the past few years, walking pads have become a popular way to boost your step count while at a computer. Some people, like Divya Balakrishnan, a yoga instructor in New York City, find the slow, rhythmic movement helps them stay focused and less stressed. “When something comes up, I'm a little bit more stable and able to handle it,” she says. Under-desk bikes and mini steppers are other options.

Another strategy is to use phone calls to go for a walk outside, pace the room, or simply stand up. “Even just standing extends your hip flexors, engages your glutes, engages your core,” Bomgren says. 

If nothing else, Rogers suggests changing your posture throughout the day by shifting forward then back in your chair, or moving how you place your legs underneath you. Even bouncing your feet can increase circulation and move the joints a little. “The more you can keep things flowing, the more energy you're going to have at the end of the day,” she says.

Have an exercise snack

Taking a five-minute walk every hour has been shown to help offset the harms of sitting. Bantham says any quick movement break is worthwhile. “If you have two minutes between meetings, use those two minutes because it all counts,” she says.  

That could look like a quick set of jump squats or crunches. It could mean running up and down the stairs as fast as you can. Or, for something even simpler, Rogers recommends standing up and sitting down 10 times. 

Even gentle movement can help balance out hours of sitting, but if you’re using these “exercise snacks” in place of traditional workouts, Bomgren recommends making them hard enough to fatigue your muscles or become breathless. “You have to create enough external stress that it actually challenges you,” she says. She suggests aiming for about an eight or nine out of 10 difficulty level. If you push hard enough, research shows that short bursts of high-intensity movement can improve your cardiometabolic health and reduce your risk of several chronic diseases.

Schedule a lunchtime workout

One benefit of working from home is having a shower and a change of clothes handy. If you have the flexibility to do an online workout video or go for a run during your lunch hour, your afternoon might benefit. “It's like starting all over for the second half of the day so you've got less of that 4 p.m. lag where you feel like, ‘I need some coffee,’" Rogers says. Getting active shortly after lunch can also help regulate your blood sugar. 

Stack habits

It’s easy to get caught up in emails and video meetings before realizing you haven’t budged in hours. To avoid this, Bomgren recommends pairing movement with things you do regularly during the work day. Maybe that’s getting in 10 push-ups anytime you fetch a cup of coffee, or stretching whenever you switch tasks. 

Bantham says some of her clients intentionally schedule meetings to end five minutes before the top of the hour. That’s a natural chance to get up for a bathroom break and do some arm circles or calf raises—whatever your body is craving—before settling back down for the next call.

Don’t feel like you need to sweat

Rogers emphasizes that moving your body during the work day doesn’t need to be “exercise.” Even simple movements can encourage healthy blood flow and keep fascia from stiffening up. For instance, Balakrishnan suggests counteracting our hunched-over-the-keyboard posture with stretches that expand the chest (by reaching your arms overhead and back so your shoulders roll open), twist the spine (by grabbing one knee with the opposite hand), and open the hips (by laying one ankle across the opposite knee and reaching the chest forward). “You can do all of these from your chair, which makes it very hard to find an excuse to not do it,” she says. Although this won’t replace a workout, it can help break up sedentary hours. 

The key is to find movements you enjoy enough to do consistently. “If you absolutely hate squats, don't choose squats to be the thing that you do between meetings,” Bantham says. Instead, maybe try a mini dance party to your favorite song, or release tension with a few deep breaths and neck rolls. It all helps. “Any activity is better than no activity,” Bantham says.

item.title: Jason Crow's Road From Paratrooper to Democratic Power Player
item.description: When he's not facing death threats, he's helping House Democrats recruit candidates

media:content.media:description: Rep. Jason Crow (D-CO) speaks to the media on Sept. 26, 2024 in Washington D.C..

item.content:encoded:
The death threats arrived almost immediately.

Representative Jason Crow, along with five other Democrats in Congress with national-­security backgrounds, had recorded a video last November reminding those working in military and intelligence roles that they did not have to follow illegal orders. A message careful to stick to the letter of the law prompted President Donald Trump to call for its makers to be arrested and charged with treason. “HANG THEM GEORGE WASHINGTON WOULD!!” read a social media post that Trump publicly shared. A federal grand jury in Washington declined the Justice Department’s effort to indict the lawmakers. That victory hasn’t mitigated Crow’s anger at how he believes the President’s response put his family’s safety at risk.

“I’m really bad at sitting in a foxhole and having people lob grenades at me,” Crow, a former paratrooper and Army Ranger, tells TIME on a June afternoon at Democratic National Committee headquarters. “I’m going to lob them back.”

The fallout from the viral video placed Crow, 47, in the strongest national spotlight since 2019, when he was a House freshman tapped to be a prosecutor in Trump’s first impeachment trial. In the interim, his stature on Capitol Hill has steadily grown, as Crow emerged as a go-to voice for his party on national security. The midterm elections could further elevate his standing, as he’s helped lead candidate recruitment for House Democrats, prioritizing veterans and others with backgrounds in national security.

In Crow’s mind, these elections will show voters that Democrats have learned how to run effectively on national-­security issues, while still hammering Republicans on the twin tentpoles of cost and corruption. At the same time, Crow says his party is in need of a hard reset before 2028—though, like many, he is still workshopping ideas for what might work.

“There is actually an opportunity to build something new—not rebuild, not go back, not try to reconstitute what once was, because Americans don’t want that,” he says.

Should Democrats take the House this fall, Crow is in prime position to be a senior member of the House Intelligence Committee’s ­majority. Should a Democrat reclaim the White House in 2028, his name is likely to come up on the short lists for Cabinet positions. He also has his eye on Colorado’s Senate seat, and is not shy about a possible White House run down the line.

First, though, Crow has to navigate this tricky political moment, one that has Democrats feeling ascendant but still staring down low approval ratings. It’s not entirely unfamiliar terrain for Crow, who rode an earlier anti-Trump wave while vowing to stand up to party leaders he viewed as failing to meet the moment. Only this time, he’s on the inside.

Impeachment and Iran

Eight years ago, Crow was one of House Democrats’ top recruits—a lawyer and veterans’ advocate who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Even still, he was far from a sure thing when he challenged Representative Mike Coffman, a fixture in Colorado Republican circles since Crow was in middle school. “This was an unwinnable race, remember?” Crow recalls with a smirk.

To show he wasn’t running against just Trump, but Washington writ large, Crow vowed not to vote for Nancy Pelosi for Speaker if Democrats won a House majority, which they did. When it came time for the vote, Crow defied the most powerful Democrat in Washington by casting his ballot for Tammy Duckworth, a fellow veteran representing Illinois in the Senate.

“I explained that this was not personal. This was part of a larger effort to usher in that next generation,” Crow recalls.

Ten months later, when it became clear that the Trump impeachment train was leaving the station for its first go-round, Pelosi rang up her former detractor. It was, Crow said later, “like being called into the principal’s office.” Pelosi needed someone with his skill set and temperament to convey the stakes of Trump’s attempts to pressure Ukraine without coming off as a partisan hack. While the House voted to impeach, the Senate declined to convict.

For Crow during that period, death threats became routine. He had an armed guard outside his house. A security detail walked his kids to school. Which brings him to last year. The security had to be called back. His “illegal orders” video brought about another round of threats—including some from Trump that Crow’s office referred to the Capitol Police, according to an email obtained by TIME.

Crow’s national-­security background has helped propel his reach in Congress, where he’s a top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee as well as the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee’s spy panel. When House Democrats needed someone to run point on a panel investigating the failed assassination against Trump in Butler, Pa., they tapped Crow. Last week, Crow and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a Washington Democrat, forced a House vote to halt the war in Iran, with the measure passing 214-208.

Recruiting "streetfighters" to Congress

But it’s his work helping Democrats win back the House that may win him the most chits. As a leader in candidate recruitment for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Crow has his hands in just about every contested race in the country, and is making a point of finding people he believes voters will view as “street fighters.”

“The oath of service I took doesn’t expire,” says JoAnna Mendoza, a retired Marine Corps drill sergeant and Crow recruit who is taking on Representative Juan Ciscomani, an Arizona Republican, in one of the top toss-up races in the country.

Mendoza has the support of Crow and the DCCC well before her primary. It’s a different story in some House races in other states where the DCCC either professed neutrality or backed a different candidate from whomever Crow endorsed through his political action committee, Service First.

Crow’s theory is that some of his preferred candidates—Marine drill sergeants, federal prosecutors—are more likely to excite those who are down on both parties.

The DCCC's chair, Rep. Suzan DelBene from Washington state, is hardly trying to curb his instincts.

“Jason brings a servant leadership ethos and a soldier’s discipline to the job. He knows that voters want fighters who put their local communities first, not undying loyalty to partisan ideology," she tells TIME. "His tireless work at recruiting, mentoring, and raising money to support candidates has been essential in our path back to the majority.”

If his instincts prove right, Crow may bring a whole raft of newcomers to Congress who are loyal to a mentor who helped get them there. Whatever Crow’s future ambitions, a cohort of fellow street fighters might come in handy.

“I have an independent streak to me,” he concedes. “But, you know, when we win, people will be pretty happy about that.”

Correction, July 27

The original version of this story misstated Crow’s rank on the House Intelligence Committee. He is a top Democrat there, but not the top Democrat on that panel.
