item.title: Chalk One Up for Ukraine
item.description: Ukraine has built a defense sector at an astonishing speed and emerged as a global player in military innovation.

media:content.media:description: A Ukrainian military ground drone travels along a road protected by anti-drone nets in Donetsk region, Ukraine, on June 20, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
It is often hard to know who is winning the war in Ukraine. The front lines scarcely budge. The air war brings regular Russian missile strikes—the most recent ones have hit Kyiv—and Ukrainian attacks that have battered Russian oil refineries and reached as far as Siberia. Ukrainian officials say the tide is turning their way; the Kremlin insists it will win a war of attrition.

In one significant way, Ukraine has already won. Some of the world’s wealthiest and most powerful nations—the United States included—are now turning to Ukraine for military assistance. Ukraine has built a defense sector at an astonishing speed and emerged as a global player in military innovation. “Ukraine needs NATO, but NATO needs Ukraine as much as the other way around,” remarked President Alexander Stubb of Finland, which joined NATO in 2023.

Beyond its implications for the war, this is a stunning achievement that will serve Ukraine well long after the guns fall silent. In President Donald Trump’s parlance, Ukraine now has a powerful “card” to play, a card it dealt itself.

From garage tech to global powerhouse

When Russia invaded Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky pleaded for foreign military aid from the West and exhorted his countrymen to build makeshift weapons for the resistance. For a time, Kyiv was grateful for pledges of American support, Bayraktar drones from Turkey, and whatever cheap weapons emerged from Ukrainian garages and warehouses.

Four and a half years later, American aid is drying up, Ukraine has replaced Bayraktar drones with more effective weapons of its own, and the country’s weapon designers have moved well beyond their low-tech garages. Ukraine’s defense technology sector is now a $7 billion industry, with many global customers and a projected annual production capacity estimated at $55 billion.

A short list of made-in-Ukraine successes includes the FP-5 Flamingo, a cruise missile with a range of more than 1,800 miles; tens of thousands of robots designed for frontline logistics and combat operations, which are minimizing risk for soldiers and are increasingly used for holding ground, firing on the enemy, and even taking prisoners; drones launched from unmanned boats to intercept and destroy Russian Shahed drones; and the “Lima” electronic warfare system, which spoofs satellite navigation signals, sending incoming missiles astray.

What began as a frantic request for outside help and garage-style innovation has evolved into a manufacturing juggernaut, large enough to support the resistance and to sell to other nations. “I’ve been arguing for many years that Ukraine would eventually become a net exporter of security,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. Ambassador to Russia, remarked in April. “That day is coming faster than I imagined.”

How the Iran war has helped Ukraine

The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran hurt Ukraine by shifting global attention away from Russia’s aggression, but that war has also been a boon for Kyiv. Gulf states, and even some American military bases in the region, turned out to be poorly prepared to fight Iranian drone and missile attacks. Ukraine had built the technology that could help.

Ukraine’s edge involves what some have called the “Ford-versus-Ferrari” problem in air defense. The U.S. and its allies in the Gulf have relied on the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Patriot missile defense systems, which can knock almost any incoming weapon out of the sky. But those systems were designed to counter heavy missiles, and they are expensive. Each Patriot missile costs roughly $5 million. Using these against $50,000 Iranian drones is, as many have noted, akin to racing a Ferrari against a Ford. Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, compared it to “throwing Ferraris at frisbees.”

Enter Ukraine, with its battle-tested counter-drone systems, which have beaten back barrages of Russian and Iranian drones at a fraction of the cost of THAAD systems and Patriots. To extend the metaphor, these are “Fords.” And they work. Zelensky has made this case to the rest of the world with great effect. In the past few months, he has signed defense export agreements with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, wealthy nations that typically turn to the U.S. for military hardware. 

Washington has gone from dismissing Zelensky to seeking deals of its own with Ukraine. After an Iranian drone attack killed six American soldiers in Kuwait in March, the Trump Administration turned to Ukraine for help. At Washington’s request, Ukraine set up its Sky Map air defense system at Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, home to more than 2,000 Americans. Two months later, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said he was pushing American firms to develop low-cost air defense interceptors within a year, and encouraged them to learn from the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

At a White House meeting last August, according to Axios, Zelensky presented a plan to exchange Ukrainian counter-drone technology for American aid. His PowerPoint included a scenario that would turn out to be prescient: Iranian drone attacks on the Gulf states and American military bases in the region. The White House rejected the offer. Even in March, Trump was dismissive, saying: “We don’t need their help in drone defense.” 

Though Ukraine still cannot envision a path into NATO, it is now selling its weapons and expertise to NATO countries and advising the alliance on military matters. During NATO exercises on Sweden’s Gotland island in May, Ukrainian drone teams overwhelmed Swedish forces, and warned the alliance that it was unprepared for modern drone warfare. 

Ukraine has opened ten weapons export centers across Europe. On July 15, the European Union and Ukraine signed a drone-production partnership. Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland announced a deal under which Ukraine would help his country build a “modern drone Armada.” Ukraine and Germany have signed an agreement focusing on drone production and battlefield technology integration. And Kyiv has signed drone deals with Norway, Denmark, and the Baltic nations. Even Japan is getting in on the Ukrainian boom: its Terra Drone company has partnered with a Ukrainian developer to scale up interceptor drone systems.

A powerful card

None of this guarantees Ukraine a victory over Russia, or even success at the negotiating table. What it does do is boost the odds that, when the guns finally fall silent, Ukraine will have a viable future and a powerful post-war “card” to play.

Were the war to end tomorrow, Ukraine would have lost territory but gained military partnerships and significant investments, along with a new engine for its security and economic future. Russia, meanwhile, would struggle to reassemble an economy that has been badly battered, one that relies almost solely on the fickle oil market and the war economy itself. 

All of which is to say: chalk one up for Ukraine. These aren’t just wins for Kyiv’s coffers, or for its ability to wreak fresh havoc on Russian targets. They are also a valuable asset that isn’t going anywhere, no matter what happens on the battlefield. For a country that will need every possible resource to rebuild, that is not just a card. It is an ace.

item.title: The Contradiction at the Heart of Disability in America
item.description: America loves seeing disabled people. It doesn’t want to pay to keep us alive, writes Steve Way.

media:content.media:description: The author in Washington, D.C. on July 24, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
I’m an actor. I also use a motorized wheelchair and a ventilator, and both of them run on Medicaid. The machine that pushes air into my lungs, the chair that moves me across a room, and the aide who gets me out of bed so I can do my job and be on television are all paid for by Medicaid. Without that coverage, I wouldn’t have a career. Instead, I would have a massive life crisis. 

I’ve spent this year in a split-screen. On one side, I’ve had the best professional run of my life. On the other, a law that’s starting to take shape is threatening to make people like me suffer and disappear. 

That contradiction ultimately comes down to how much our country believes a disabled person is worth.

On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. By the Congressional Budget Office’s own accounting, its Medicaid provisions cut around $1 trillion in federal spending over a decade, and will leave an estimated 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034. Count the rest of the law’s health provisions, and the coverage loss climbs to an estimated 10 million. The Center for American Progress notes the spending cuts almost exactly match the law’s other half: about $1 trillion in tax cuts flowing to the top 1% of households, nearly half of that to roughly 200,000 households making more than $2 million a year. 

Approximately a trillion dollars taken from the care of poor and disabled people, and roughly a trillion handed to the richest households in the country. 

Then, there’s the cost no budget table ever lists. Before the bill reached its final, larger form, three physician-researchers published a peer-reviewed analysis in the Annals of Internal Medicine projecting what the cuts would do to actual lives. Their mid-range estimate:16,642 additional preventable deaths a year. 

If the losses fall hardest on disabled, high-cost enrollees rather than spreading evenly, the cuts could go even deeper. In a law built to find savings, the most expensive bodies to keep alive are the most efficient place to look. The math suggests that I cost a lot, and the bill was written by people looking for things that cost a lot. 

We must not trade disabled peoples’ lives in exchange for tax cuts for the ultra-wealthy. And we must not sacrifice all of the progress the U.S. has made. 

On July 26, 1990, a Republican president signed the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), the world’s first comprehensive civil rights law for disabled people, and a law older than me. George H.W.  Bush stood on the South Lawn and promised disabled people “independence, freedom of choice, control of their lives, the opportunity to blend fully and equally into the rich mosaic of the American mainstream.” 

Yesterday marked its 36th anniversary. The show I’m proudly in, Furious, premieres today. 

The ADA said disabled people have a right to live in America. The new law cuts the exact funding that helps many of us live, including the home-based services that keep disabled people like myself out of nursing facilities and in their own homes, which is the precise independence the ADA was written to protect. 

Representation has quietly become a consolation prize. Even though the percentage is still low, there are more disabled people on television than ever, and I’m grateful to be one of them. But the applause and the cuts are happening simultaneously, to the same people, and almost no one with power experiences that as a contradiction. 

You can be celebrated on a streaming service and defunded by a signature in the same summer. The issue: being seen is not the same as being kept alive. 

Many people genuinely believe those are the same thing. Visibility is a form of protection and a society putting disabled people on television would surely not also strip away the thing that gets them out of bed. It’s a comforting belief, but in modern America, it is false. Visibility is cheap. It costs the country nothing. Care is what costs, and care is what was cut. 

America has gotten very good at the gesture of inclusion and very comfortable with the substance of abandonment. Too often, we perform the first loudly enough to drown out the second. 

Disabled people see this gap with clarity. I’m telling you what it looks like from here because the view is unobstructed, and because I am, for now, still in a position to describe it. 

I’ll spend this month promoting a television show, marking 36 years of a promise, and watching my own healthcare coverage get more precarious, doing the arithmetic on my care in the back of my mind while I smile for cameras. I’ve got some great red carpet one-liners lined up. 

I’ve built a career on finding the joke in exactly this kind of absurdity, and I have to find it here, because the alternative is worse.

item.title: House of the Dragon Just Unceremoniously Killed Off a Main Character. It Was the Right Move
item.description: And his death was as unceremonious as they come

media:content.media:description: Heading into battle in Episode 6 of House of the Dragon Season 3.

item.content:encoded:
Warning: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of House of the Dragon Season 3.

After two seasons of cementing himself as one of the most hated characters in Westeros history (which, as Game of Thrones fans know, has no shortage of reprehensible monsters), Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) ultimately went out with little more than a whimper in Episode 6 of House of the Dragon Season 3.

Following his declaration in Episode 5 that he intended to die a warrior's death by leading his men on a suicide mission into the path of Team Black's massive army of Rivermen and Winter Wolves, Cole was erased from the board within the first 10 minutes of Sunday's installment. The episode opened with Cole and his remaining Greens falling into a trap set by young Lord Oscar Tully (Archie Barnes) and Lord Roderick Dustin (Tommy Flanagan) that saw a host of Rivermen play dead in order to lure their enemy into battle. Although Cole's forces triumphed in the scuffle, they soon realized the real trick was that they were surrounded by the full strength of the Black army.

Cole attempted to bargain for his men's lives by promising surrender and, when that offer was refused, put forth a bid to decide the battle by facing Oscar and Roderick in two vs. one combat. But Team Black obviously had no plans of letting Cole go out in the blaze of glory he so greatly desired. Without waiting for either lord to even deign to respond, archer Alysanne Blackwood (Annie Shapero) let loose three arrows that struck Cole down, unceremoniously killing him. Their army then advanced on his men to slaughter them.

Those who have read George R. R. Martin's Fire & Blood will recognize this event as the massacre known as the Butcher's Ball. And in the book, it's made abundantly clear Team Black meant for Cole to die as undignified a death as possible. As one Riverlands knight bluntly remarks to Cole's dead body, "I'll have no songs about how brave you died, Kingmaker."

In House of the Dragon, it was ironically Cole himself who set the scene for his anticlimactic demise—because really, how often does a character in the Thrones universe actually get what they want? "I am the realm's greatest warrior," he told Ser Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in Episode 5. "And I will die as such. Clear-eyed. Unbent. Glorious in battle. And not in their service, finally. But in my own. And they will sing songs of it. And Queen Alicent herself will hear them."

Despite proving himself to be the Dance of the Dragons' most hypocritical player, by shifting his allegiance to Alicent (Olivia Cooke) and the Greens back in Season 1, Cole managed to convince himself he was walking the path of righteousness. No matter how deplorable his actions were, in his mind, everything he did was to uphold honor, duty, and the law. But after witnessing the devastating power of dragonfire firsthand at the Battle of Rook's Rest in Season 2, Cole's view of the conflict began to spiral into nihilism. In the end, the only way he felt he could leave his mark on the world was to go down swinging in battle.

"Criston Cole started as a soldier before the 20-year stretch that he spent at King’s Landing—that’s how he started, and that’s how he wants to finish," Frankel told Variety of his character's motivations in Season 3. "In his mind, the only honest version of himself is the soldier. Everything else is pretense; the diplomat is pretense; the Hand of the King, there’s a level of pretense; Lord Commander of the Kingsguard, there’s a level of pretense. I suppose they’re all psychological, brain-led jobs. He isn’t that way, he’s very much led by his sword and his fighting instinct. The idea that that’s how he will be remembered, I think, feels honest."

But Cole doesn't get the poetic, honorable last stand he thinks he deserves, reinforcing the futility of common soldiers fighting a war of nobles and stripping him of the fantasy of a worthy legacy in his final moments. Seems like Alicent will never hear those songs, after all.

item.title: What to Know About the Deadly Wildfires in Western Europe
item.description: More than 300,000 people were evacuated because of wildfires in France and Spain, with fire crews battling the blazes for several days.
item.content:encoded:
More than 300,000 people were evacuated and at least one person killed because of wildfires in France and Spain, with fire crews battling the blazes for several days.

The two countries are facing massive wildfires that began last week amid successive heat waves in Europe that produced record high temperatures in several countries and led to thousands of excess deaths.

Read More: Europe's Heat Wave Fuels Fears of a Record-Hot Year

In France, a major fire broke out in Saumos in Gironde last Wednesday, and a separate fire began near Biscarrosse in the Landes department the next day. Several fires broke out in Spain last Wednesday, including one in Toledo that spread into Madrid’s Villa del Prado and another in Ávila. Fires in Madrid, Castellón, and Manises broke out in the following days.

Both countries had already faced deadly wildfires earlier in the summer.

Here’s what to know about the wildfires affecting France and Spain.

What has been the impact?

Fire crews were dealing with a 280-km perimeter of fire covering 77,000 hectares across Madrid, Ávila, and Toledo, Spain’s Secretary-General for Civil Protection and Emergencies Virginia Barcones told state broadcaster TVE.

The Spanish regions of Madrid, Ávila, and Valencia were among the worst affected areas. The government declared a national emergency in Madrid and Ávila on Thursday evening, extending it to Toledo on Saturday. It was Spain’s first such declaration over wildfires and only the second overall, after the nationwide blackout in April 2025. The government deployed 1,200 and 400 vehicles to fight the fires in Madrid and Ávila, respectively. At least 37 sections of road were closed to traffic on Sunday morning because of fires across seven provinces or regions.

Spain recorded its first death from the latest wildfires on Saturday when a 78-year-old man was killed in a fire in Manises, near Valencia. The victim, who reportedly had reduced mobility, was found dead in his car.

Several major fronts of the wildfires affecting Madrid and Ávila were contained by Sunday morning, according to Spain’s Military Emergencies Unit, although the fires remained active. The wildfire risk also remained high in the eastern and southern parts of the country, according to Spain’s meteorological agency, Aemet. That risk is expected to go up in the coming days as the temperature warms this week, Aemet said.

In France, around 55,000 people were ordered to evacuate villages near Bordeaux, including Le Barp, Marcheprime, Biganos, Mios, and Cestas, overnight on Saturday. In total, more than 250,000 people in southwestern France were forced to evacuate in recent days.

In Gironde, at least 240 homes were destroyed as of Sunday, officials said. The fire spread to within 15 km from the edge of Bordeaux’s metropolitan area and around 25 to 30 km from the city center. Bordeaux officials said they are evaluating the situation but that there are no immediate plans to evacuate the city.

Wildfires in France have also disrupted the Tour de France, as organizers shortened its final stage from 133 km to 89 km so security personnel can be redeployed to affected areas.

France’s meteorological agency warned that wildfire danger remained high across many departments despite a slight improvement over the weekend, especially as another heat wave is expected to worsen fire conditions in the coming days.

How is climate change exacerbating wildfire risks?

Much of Europe has been affected by successive heat waves that have raised the risk of wildfires. With temperatures expected to rise again and little rain forecast in many fire-affected areas, that danger is only expected to increase this week.

Global warming has made heat waves more prevalent and more intense, with Europe warming at twice the global average rate since the 1980s. The extreme heat increases evaporation and plant water loss, worsening drought and drying out vegetation which creates more fuel for wildfires.

Spain recorded 32 major forest fires so far this year. That’s a significant increase from last year, when the country recorded seven over the same time period.

“I’d once again like to urge people to take utmost care and to stay up to date,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Sunday. “The Iberian Peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency.”

Heat waves also make it more difficult to contain fires, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told La Tribune Dimanche on Sunday. Dry weather, high temperatures, and dense ground vegetation make the fires spread rapidly once they begin.

Earlier this month, other deadly wildfires struck France and Spain. At least 13 people were killed in the Los Gallardos fire in southern Spain and a 22-year-old volunteer firefighter died while battling a vegetation fire in Savoie, France.

How to stay safe

People in affected areas should follow official instructions and evacuate immediately if ordered.

Anyone in the E.U. who suspects a new fire should call 112 if it is safe to do so, and move away from the flames toward an area with little vegetation. If smoke or ash is present, residents should limit outdoor activities.

Read More: How to Safely Lower Your Body Temperature In Extreme Heat

The Madrid regional government said, as of Sunday, 2,468 evacuees were receiving assistance at 15 temporary shelters, where local authorities supplied meals, beds, and basic hygiene products.

French municipalities have also opened temporary shelters. Bordeaux officials said around 3,500 evacuees were staying at its exhibition center shelter on Saturday morning.

item.title: Wildfire Disruptions to the Tour de France Show How Climate Change Is Shaping Sports
item.description: Tadej Pogačar's fifth Tour de France victory came after last-minute course changes due to wildfires, underscoring how climate change is influencing major sporting events.
item.content:encoded:
What should have been a standout moment in the world of sports was almost overshadowed on Sunday as 27-year-old Slovenian cyclist Tadej Pogačar took home his fifth Tour de France amid a last-minute course change in response to wildfires raging in the country’s southwest region. The disruption is one of a growing number of examples of extreme weather forcing changes to global sporting events.

For the final stage of the world’s most prestigious cycling race, what was meant to be a 133-kilometer (82-mile) ride was shortened to 89 km (55.3 miles). Riders were presented in Thoiry before being transported by team buses to Paris, where the race consisted entirely of circuits around the French capital, including two additional laps of the Champs-Élysées.

The change was announced late Saturday. Officials said it would allow emergency first responders and security personnel to shift their attention from the race to the wildfires. 

"In a spirit of national solidarity with the areas and communities affected, it was decided to adapt the route for the final stage," the event's organizers said in a statement.

The disruption was just the latest in a series of extreme weather events that have altered this year’s competition. Earlier in the race, stage nine was shortened by 30 km (18 miles) due to extreme heat.

A number of the participants commented on the impact of extreme heat this year, including Pogačar, who suggested having cyclists race earlier, when the heat is less intense, or altering the race calendar. 

“If I had the power I would change all the calendar and not race in July and August in hot places,” he said. 

The race director replied that such a schedule shift would never be possible, as it could impact critical factors of the event, from obtaining government authorizations to negatively impacting viewership—and therefore the revenue—when the race is aired by broadcasters.

Read More: How Europe's Extreme Heat Waves Have Impacted the Tour de France

As of Saturday night, dozens of wildfires were burning in the southwest of France, near Bordeaux. Over 197,000 people had already been evacuated throughout the country, while its neighbor, Spain, saw some 80,000 evacuated.

Research shows climate change is fostering the conditions that allow wildfires to spread rapidly, as hotter temperatures and drier vegetation make many landscapes more flammable. In the last four years, the amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe increased by 57%, according to new data from the World Health Organization. 

In Spain and Portugal alone, the number of wildfires has more than doubled since last year.

Europe, which is warming faster than any other continent, is in the midst of a particularly dry, hot summer, creating ideal conditions for wildfires. Following a heatwave in June, data showed that France recorded at least 5,700 excess deaths during the month. 

Two weeks later, at the start of this year’s Tour de France, the average temperature along the course was 87.4°F—far surpassing the previous record of 78.6°F in 2022.

Climate Change Is Forcing Sports to Adapt

The Tour de France is not the only sporting event that’s been forced to contend with the impact of climate extremes. 

“Recent years have been a turning point for sport, just because so many sporting events have been impacted by climate change,” says Madeleine Orr, assistant professor of Sport Ecology at the University of Toronto. In 2020, tennis player Dalila Jakupovic collapsed on court during the Australian Open due to poor air quality because of wildfires. Soon after, the Tokyo Olympics saw athletes sweltering in 90°F temperatures. 

Extreme weather has become impossible to ignore—and organizers are being forced to adapt. 

For the first time in the history of the World Cup, FIFA began mandating three-minute “hydration breaks” as games across North America carried on amid high temperatures and humidity. The tournament's final was threatened by hazardous wildfire smoke drifting over New York from hundreds of fires burning in Ontario, Canada, as well as northern Minnesota.

The NFL is increasingly favoring roofed and domed stadiums, with nearly two-thirds of league venues expected to see updates by 2030—to the tune of billions of dollars in construction. And in June, a “heat hazard” went into effect for Formula 1’s Austrian Grand Prix, meaning that drivers would be required to have a “driver cooling system” in place in order to compete.

While the organizations behind some of sports’ most popular events are looking to counteract the effects of climate change, athletes are also forced to adapt their training to better acclimate to heat. In the Tour de France, some teams prepared ice baths for riders to utilize immediately after completing a portion of the race. Laura Schifter explained in a recent opinion piece for TIME that even children’s sports will likely be impacted, reshaping the lifelong habits and mindsets young athletes develop.

And the changes ultimately affect those who attend the sporting events. There’s the added strain of attending outdoor sporting events in extreme weather—which often involves long lines leading into the events and long hours in the sun in the stands. There may also be financial consequences, as investments in new facilities or weather adaptations can increase operating costs, which in some cases wind up passed down to fans. Or they might not get to attend at all: Earlier this month, spectators were asked not to watch the last 40 km (25 miles) of the third stage of the Tour de France to reduce the demand on security personnel and free up more resources for the wildfires.

Adaptation measures are only going to become more common in our warming world, experts tell TIME. 

“This is the coolest summer that's going to be in our lifetimes,” says Samuel Hampton, senior researcher at the University of Oxford’s Environmental Change Institute. “It's only going to get hotter and hotter for the rest of our lives, and I think the [Tour de France] is already straining in terms of how it can deal with this heat.”

“It's only going to become more challenging,” he added.

item.title: Berlin Pride Attack Suspect Dies in Police Confrontation After Daylong Manhunt
item.description: Berlin Police shot and killed the suspect who allegedly rammed his vehicle into a crowd at Berlin Pride on Saturday night, leaving one dead and dozens injured.

media:content.media:description: Emergency personnel and police gather in Berlin on July 26, 2026, following a deadly attack at the annual Christopher Street Day festivities.

item.content:encoded:
Authorities shot and killed the suspect believed to be responsible for a deadly attack at Berlin Pride on Saturday, according to police. The suspect, identified Sunday as Abdul Ballout, allegedly plowed a vehicle into a crowd of revelers, leaving one woman dead and at least 29 injured. Officials have said that the attack was likely motivated by Islamist extremism.

“According to current findings, he is said to have rushed toward our emergency forces with a stabbing weapon, after which police firearms were used,” the Berlin Police said in a post on X, confirming that the confrontation occurred at approximately 6 p.m. local time Sunday. It went on to say that resuscitation efforts at the scene proved unsuccessful.

Suspect Believed Responsible for Deadly Attack on Berlin Pride

The confrontation followed a nearly daylong manhunt. Alexander Dobrindt, the German Interior Minister, said at a press conference on Sunday that “large-scale” search operations spanned train stations, airports, and the borders, as officials searched for the man seen fleeing the scene following the previous evening’s deadly attack. 

The incident occurred around 10 p.m. local time, promptly ending the remainder of the scheduled events for the nation’s annual Christopher Street Day celebration. The LGBTQ+ event, also referred to as Berlin Pride, is named for the New York City street that hosted the 1969 Stonewall riots—widely credited for launching the modern gay rights movement. The festivities included a concert on Saturday evening near Tiergarten, a large park in the center of the city.

As hundreds of thousands gathered, a white minivan plowed through a side street adjacent to the park, striking pedestrians before crashing into a tree. The driver exited the vehicle and may have continued his assault on foot before fleeing the scene. Authorities believe he wielded a stabbing instrument, due to the nature of the injuries sustained by several passersby after the suspect exited the van.

“Everything we are seeing here indicates an Islamist terror attack,” Dobrindt said early Sunday.

Read More: Why Car-Rammings Are on the Rise—and So Hard to Prevent

A Berlin Police spokesperson told reporters in the immediate aftermath of the attack that there had been coordinated security measures in place for the Pride event.

"We meticulously prepared this event together with the organizer. We have an incredible number of personnel deployed,” he said, noting that extensive access barriers had been set up to prevent vehicles from entering the event grounds.

A Berlin Fire Service spokesperson told media outlets at the scene that at least 11 victims suffered life-threatening or serious injuries. None of the victims have been publicly identified.

“Berlin is the city of freedom—and our freedom has been attacked in the most horrific way today,” Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner said in a statement Sunday, while promising that authorities were responding to the suspected terror attack with “utmost urgency.”

Later that evening, Wegner confirmed to German broadcaster rbb that the suspect “had been apprehended.” 

"The fact that the Berlin police have the suspect within 24 hours is a major success for the investigating authorities," he said.

Who Is Abdul Ballout?

Police on Saturday released a photo of the suspect who was originally identified only by his first name and last initial, in compliance with German privacy laws. “Abdul B.” was described as a 21-year-old German-born citizen. Police described him as having a slim build, with black hair, and standing approximately 1.9 meters tall (6-foot-2). He was last seen wearing a black hoodie with white pants, per the police report.

Dobrindt said on Sunday that “the suspect has in the past come to the attention of authorities.”

“He has committed various crimes. He has been radicalized in the past. He belongs to the Islamist scene,” Dobrindt continued.

The Berlin Public Prosecutor’s Office released additional details Sunday evening, upon taking over the investigations. It said that Ballout had been found guilty of assaulting a victim in a schoolyard in 2019 and of robbing an individual, along with an accomplice, in 2020. He was then convicted of assault and robbery in juvenile court in 2022.

Ballout allegedly “developed the desire to join the armed struggle of ISIS” in 2025, the press release continued.

He traveled to Lebanon and allegedly attempted to contact ISIS there, it said, but was arrested and sentenced to three months’ imprisonment for “incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.” 

According to prosecutors, he returned to Germany after his release and was placed under arrest. The court had “found it proven” that he had published Islamic State propaganda on his Instagram account in 2024. In May 2026, he was sentenced to 22 months in prison. The court considered suspending the sentence because of the time he had already spent in pretrial detention and in prison in Lebanon. He was released under probation supervision while a final decision on the suspension was delayed for six months.

“The Public Prosecutor's Office had requested a longer, non-probationary sentence for the juvenile and the continuation of the arrest warrant,” its press release on Sunday evening said.

Police searched his address on July 3 upon suspicion of a Weapons Act violation, but only discovered a toy gun, so “the case was subsequently dismissed,” the statement continued.

That same residence was searched following the Berlin Pride attack early Sunday, but the suspect was not on the premises. 

Is the Attack Part of a Larger Pattern of Extremist Terrorism in Germany?

The threat level in Germany remained at its recently declared “high threat level” on Sunday. It was established after intelligence pointed toward potential attack plans, according to the Interior Ministry. 

Investigators had not determined whether Ballout acted alone as of Sunday evening. Police said they had not ruled out additional suspects.

“According to the current state of the investigation, there is at least one suspect,” the Berlin Police department posted while seeking public assistance. Dobrindt also commented on Sunday, “We cannot rule out the possibility that further terror attacks and such terrible acts might take place.”

The heightened threat level aligns with assessments published in the June 30 publication of the Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz (BfV) Annual Report on the Protection of the Constitution, which states that "the threat posed by Islamist terrorism in Germany remains high." The report is part of a greater effort by the intelligence organization to “raise awareness about the level of threat posed to state and society.”

Its data shows that while the Islamic extremist following in 2025 was composed of 28,645 individuals (up from 28,280 the year prior), approximately 9,110 of them were “violence oriented” (down from 9,540 in 2024).

German intelligence has long warned that hostility toward LGBTQ+ people is "an integral part of all Islamist extremist ideologies," though the motives for the Berlin Pride attack have yet to be determined.

The BfV report explains that extremists see tolerance toward sexual and gender diversity as an imported Western value “which allegedly aims at destroying the Islamic community.”

“Against this backdrop, Islamist extremists spread hate propaganda and systematically exploit this topic as an additional field of agitation in their fight against supposedly morally ‘misguided’ Western values,” it continued.

Government representatives sought to reassure the public later that day in light of the latest assessments.

“Let us not be afraid,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a public statement on Sunday afternoon. “These actions have one aim. They want to divide our society. They want to take away from us our most important assets: our openness, and our freedom.”

He also expressed support for the victims and their families and gratitude toward first responders on the scene, assuring that authorities would move quickly to capture the suspect.

“There are more of us, we are stronger, and we will stay together,” he said, addressing his countrymen. “That is the most important thing in such a difficult hour.”

item.title: Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn on AI, User Motivation, and Expanding Beyond Languages
item.description: TIME spoke with Luis von Ahn about Duolingo’s story, user engagement, and how he’s approaching AI integration.

media:content.media:description: Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn

item.content:encoded:
When Luis von Ahn was 8 years old, growing up in Guatemala City, his mother bought him a computer. He was upset because he actually wanted a Nintendo, he recalls. “But you know, it changed my life because I learned how to use a computer.” Developing that skill eventually led to his creation of the educational app Duolingo, which is used by millions around the world to learn languages, and now other subjects, such as math and music. The company went public in 2021 and is currently valued at $5.7 billion. 

“Education has always been a big thing for me,” says von Ahn, 47. His mother, a doctor and single parent, didn’t earn much, but spent any spare money she had on ensuring von Ahn had access to the best education in Guatemala, he says. “The other kids in my neighborhood probably went to public school. It was very clear that I was years ahead of them in terms of what I was learning, and that always stuck with me,” he says. “And that's probably the biggest reason why we started Duolingo. The idea is to try to give education to everyone, regardless of whether you don't have a lot of money or you have a lot of money, you can use the same system.” Von Ahn believes the app has achieved that goal, and says its users range from across the socioeconomic spectrum. 

TIME spoke with von Ahn in May about Duolingo’s story, user engagement, and how he’s approaching AI integration. 

This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Tell me a bit about the evolution of Duolingo.

We started very small in 2011. We wanted to do something that would give equal access to education to everyone. At first, we didn't want to teach languages. At first, we thought we wanted to teach math, but we decided to teach languages, and the reason for that was because of English. In almost every country in the world, if you know English, you can make more money. There are a little under 2 billion people in the world learning English. Math has a billion people learning it. So English is basically the most learned subject that I know of in the whole world. So we thought, OK, let's do a thing that teaches languages for free. We launched it. It was very successful from the minute we launched it. It became the most downloaded app in the education category, and it has been since then. And we reached all kinds of really amazing numbers relatively early on. For example, at some point, there were more people learning languages on Duolingo in the U.S. than there are people learning languages across all U.S. high schools combined, and now that's true in most countries in the world. Not in every country—particularly in China, it's not yet true—but in most countries we teach more people languages than the public education system. So we're very proud of that. 

For the first four or five years, we made no money. We didn't have any ads. There was no subscription. Nothing. It was just free. Then we started monetizing around 2017, but one of the crazy things that happened is that we had hired all these people, and they had come to work at Duolingo to give free education. And when I said to everyone, we need to make money to sustain ourselves, there was a revolt. People did not want to—most of the employees were like, “Why? Why do we need to make money?” Which is crazy if you think about it, but I had to explain to them that you actually have to pay salaries, and that's how we have to make money, etc. But eventually, we found a good way to make money, which is our freemium model: everybody can use Duolingo entirely for free. But if you don't pay, you have to see some ads, and if you don't like ads, you can pay to subscribe, and it gets rid of the ads.

That worked, and then after that, we started at least being self-sustaining. At some point, we became profitable. We're now a publicly traded company, so we're very happy with that. The other thing that has happened over time is we've added more subjects. We started with just languages, but now we have math, music, and chess, and we're very happy with those. I'm particularly excited about math. I think over time, hopefully, it'll become almost as large as languages. Languages are much larger, but I'm hoping that math at some point will become as large as it.

Is English the most popular language? 

Yeah, for sure. Half of our users are learning English.

And where is it most used?

We have users in every single country in the world. The largest market is the U.S. in terms of number of users. Second is China, and then third [place] oscillates between Brazil, the U.K., and Germany. 

Are there complications to operating in China?

Yes. We're fine now, but China has a lot of regulation, and we have to go through that, but we're happy. China's not the number one fastest growing country, but it is relatively fast growing, and our expectation is that within one or two years China will be our largest market. It's just growing really fast. There's just a lot of people in China, also a lot of people who want to learn English. So you keep growing.

How many languages have you learned, or are you learning? 

I got pretty good at French to the point where I can watch TV shows in French. My pronunciation is not particularly good, but I can watch TV shows pretty well. I am currently learning Swedish because my wife is Swedish, and now Swedish is an excellent language. It just turns out not a particularly useful language to learn because all Swedes seem to know English. But I am learning it because my wife is Swedish. I'm not as good as I am at French.

I have to confess I don't use Duolingo, but I did speak to some friends who use it and got some feedback. A couple of things that I heard a few times were that they don't like the guilt-tripping constant reminders, and also the need to pay to progress… 

You don't need to pay to progress. You need to pay to turn off ads. And if you don't pay, you sort of cannot do too much per hour. That's basically it.

But there's also the AI function… 

Oh yeah, as in, you have to pay if you want to do the practicing conversation with AI. You have to pay because that also costs us money. Yeah.

I'm sure you hear similar feedback. How do you take that on board and how do you integrate that into improving the app?

Well, a couple of things. In terms of the guilt-tripping, we try a lot of things. The thing about learning something by yourself—and this is really what has made us the most popular education app in the world—the hardest thing about learning something by yourself is staying motivated. It's just really hard to stay motivated. Most people will tell you that they want to learn something, but their actions don't say the same thing. I mean, their actions are [that] they're going to go to Instagram or TikTok or whatever. One of the main things I've learned here at Duolingo over the last 15 years is what people say, what people do, and what people think—completely different things. So people will tell you they really want to learn something, etc. But it's very hard to stay motivated to learn something like a language. To learn a language to a relatively good point takes hundreds, if not thousands, of hours. That is just the case. There's no faster way to do that. Your brain needs that many hours to learn it. So we need to find ways to get people to continue doing it, and we just try everything we can. We try to make it fun. Try to make it as gamified as possible. We send you reminders. Some of the reminders are guilt-tripping, and it just turns out this works. And that's the idea. The idea is to try to get you to be motivated to continue working. I mean, learning.

It sounds like your workforce is very passionate…

Mission driven. Yes. 

There was a story about assessment of employees based on AI usage, which was rolled back. What happened and what did you learn from that experience?

Last year I sent a memo internally that, honestly internally it was not controversial. I mean, it was like, “Hey, we’ve got to use AI in as [many] places as we can.” There was one part that, at the time was not controversial, but we have since flipped, which is we're going to assess people's performance based on their use of AI. That's not going to be the only thing, but one of the things I look at is are you using AI or not? Because we really do believe that AI can make you a lot more productive. I sent that memo. Externally, people read that memo and thought that I was going to fire all our employees. This is actually not what happened. We didn't fire anybody. We in fact hired more employees last year, and part of the reason is it's just now an employee is way more valuable than before because one employee with AI can just do way more than a single employee before AI. So I want to keep hiring, but internally, what we learned over the last year was that there were people who did their job, and they had a lot of impact. But they're like, “AI doesn't really apply to my job. Do you want me to just use AI for no reason?” And they had very good arguments. So, we've gone back to just, your performance is based on the impact you have on the company, regardless of what you do. So yeah, we shouldn't have done that, but we did.

You talked about offering something to users that isn't Instagram or TikTok. There are people who are also thinking about how they use AI and even not wanting to use it. How do you balance improving the app using AI integration against keeping those loyal users who like using Duolingo because it's not social media or ChatGPT?

Ultimately, our goal is to teach you things that take a long time to learn. That's our goal. It turns out AI can really help us teach you those things much better. A really good example is conversational practice. Before AI, there was no way for you to practice conversation on Duolingo, and the only way we could have done it before AI was to pair you up with another human. But this is one of those cases where people say they want to talk to another human in a language that they are not comfortable with, but people do not actually talk to another human in a language that they're not comfortable with. We tried many times. I believe about 5% of humanity's population is willing to do that, and the other 90% to 95% doesn't actually want to. Even though they say they do, they don't actually want to do that because it just requires too much. People are ashamed. Before AI, we simply could not get you to practice conversation. It just was a hole in your learning. Now with AI, you can actually fully practice conversation, and that you learn the language better. So, for our usage of AI, we have this golden rule internally in the company, which is we are only going to use AI for the benefit of our learners, and so that's it. In fact, the overwhelming majority of our usage of AI is either in speeding up our development process or in teaching better. And so, I understand that some people may not love using ChatGPT, etc. But you know, ultimately, we're just trying to teach you better.

item.title: ‘Cockroach Movement’ Forces Out India’s Education Minister
item.description: Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday in response to rising pressure from student-led protests.

media:content.media:description: Supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25, 2026 in New Delhi, India.

item.content:encoded:
Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday amid mounting pressure from the “Cockroach Movement,” which demanded major government reforms—starting with his departure. Student activists accused Pradhan of failing to safeguard a competitive medical school exam, the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), after authorities concluded that its contents had been leaked online.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) started as a parody account on social media after Indian authorities invalidated the annual medical school entry exam in May. Its name alludes to a comment made by Chief Justice Surya Kant during an unrelated hearing the same month, in which he compared young unemployed people to "cockroaches” and “parasites.”

However, the CJP quickly established itself as a formidable movement as anti-government sentiment erupted in the wake of the NEET scandal. The page gained millions of followers, and its founder began organizing protests in late June.  

Read More: What Is the Youth-Led ‘Cockroach Movement’ Staging Mass Protests in India?

How a Leaked Exam Sparked a National Movement

Over 2 million prospective students had taken the three-hour exam, according to the BBC. However, an exam coach noticed that a “guess paper”—or practice test—being circulated online seemed to closely match the exam itself, prompting an investigation. Police ultimately concluded that the questions had been leaked. They also discovered that some individuals paid as much as 5,000 rupees (about $52) to access the “guess paper” on WhatsApp, the Indian Express reported.

News that the exam results had been voided distressed many of the test-takers. The medical school system in India offered fewer than 130,000 slots for the undergraduate medical program this year, according to India’s National Medical Commission, making the selection process extremely competitive. The stakes are considerable, especially for those with limited financial resources. After the exam was discredited, at least 20 students died by suicide, according to Agence France-Presse. Protesters blamed the deaths on what they described as systemic failures in India's education system, and directed much of their anger toward Pradhan.

In a statement posted to social media after he stepped down, Pradhan said that the government would be switching to a computer-based testing model in the future to help prevent fraud and confirmed that a replacement exam had been successfully completed in June.

“India’s youth power is the real strength of this nation,” he wrote. 

Without accepting fault, he explained that he had agreed to step down in order to prevent “anti-national forces” from exploiting the upheaval. 

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP, celebrated the resignation with fellow protesters in New Delhi on Saturday.

“It's a victory for the people of India,” Dipke said to the crowd. He later posted an image of India’s Constitution on social media, with the caption: “Thank you.”

How the Protests Forced the Government to the Table

Despite police orders not to march on Parliament, tens of thousands of protesters attempted to do so last week and clashed with local authorities. The following day, they escalated their efforts by attempting to block public transportation, setting up barricades at the entrance of key metro stations and disrupting travel for millions of daily commuters. The police used tear gas and batons to disperse protesters, sparking public outrage. 

Activist Sonam Wangchuk was then forcibly taken to hospital after 26 days of a hunger strike meant to bring attention to protesters’ demands. He told local media outlets that he concluded his campaign after receiving assurances that the “issue of accountability” for the failures of the exam would be discussed by Parliament.

Upon hearing the news of the Education Minister’s resignation on Saturday, he told reporters that he welcomed the move.

"This is a victory for democracy that we witnessed today,” he said. “I congratulate and thank our CJP team who first raised this issue, as well as the volunteers who supported them, the students, youth, and elders from across the country who stood up for democracy.”

"I hope we maintain this peace and that no wrongdoing occurs anywhere in the future. We need to work on reforms. A nation isn't built by resignation alone," he added.

On the advice of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Indian President Droupadi Murmu appointed Pralhad Joshi—who already oversees the ministries of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, along with New and Renewable Energy—to oversee the Ministry of Education “in addition to his existing portfolio,” which is a typical arrangement in India following a Cabinet vacancy and does not preclude a later permanent appointment.

Joshi addressed the exam leak in May, saying, “The reforms are needed, we are bringing them, but they cannot be done within a year. By next year, technology-driven examination will be there."

CJP Spokesperson Saurav Das said in an interview with local media ANI following the president’s announcement that the party members will be meeting the new education minister “very soon.”

“Whoever becomes the Education Minister should know that the youth are watching. They will demand accountability,” Das said. “So, when the time comes, work in the interest of the youth. Stop paper leaks.”

What Comes Next for the CJP?

The CJP established its list of demands on May 16. In addition to calling for Pradhan’s resignation, the CJP asked for compensation of 10 million rupees ($104,000) for each student who died by suicide following the leak. 

They also sought greater legislative oversight of the educational system, gender equity in government roles, a fully independent media, and certain reforms to the electoral and political system—such as creating a 20-year ban on politicians switching parties before seeking election.

Adding to those mandates, the CJP last week asked that the central government drop any potential charges against protesters, after claiming that several had been “illegally detained” by police. 

Following Pradhan’s resignation, representatives from the CJP met with officials from the Indian government to discuss the rest of the party’s demands. In a press conference following the meeting, Das said on Saturday that the negotiations had been successful.

"All our demands have been accepted,” he said, without elaboration. “We request the protesters to withdraw immediately and return home peacefully."

The CJP added during the press conference on Saturday that representatives from the movement would meet with officials again in four weeks to work on broader reforms. Its spokesperson told local media that the fight for a transparent educational system is far from over. 

He said that members of the CJP conveyed to officials that if the issues are not addressed, the protesters will reconvene “and demand accountability.”

item.title: Understanding The Fraught Politics Of Powering AI
item.description: Growing anxiety over electricity bills, on the rise in part because of the AI-driven infrastructure buildout, has quickly become a liability for industry and politicians alike

media:content.media:credit: Photo by Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images
media:content.media:description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an event about the Ratepayer Protection Pledge at the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington D.C. on July 23

item.content:encoded:
Sitting at the Environmental Protection Agency with a mix of CEOs and cabinet officials, President Trump announced this week that a group of more than 200 stakeholders including governors, utility companies, and data center developers had signed up for his Ratepayer Protection Pledge, vowing to protect consumers from the rising costs of electricity.

The announcement is an attempt to hold off the growing anxiety over electricity bills, which are on the rise in part because of the AI-driven infrastructure buildout. The anxiety has quickly become a liability for industry and politicians alike.


But there’s also little doubt that the pledge, which is voluntary with no enforcement mechanism, is just tinkering around the edges of the issue. And the slower policymakers are to take decisive, substantive action, the more likely it becomes that today’s targeted fixes give way to demands for wholesale restructuring.

Two days before Trump launched his updated pledge, I moderated a panel at the Aspen Ideas Climate summit in Chicago addressing issues of rising electricity costs and reliability issues on the grid. The most interesting exchange came over the needed scale of solutions. 


Allison Clements, a former member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, argued that states and utilities should move quickly to insulate customers from the cost of data centers, citing a range of regulatory tweaks. University of Chicago economist Michael Greenstone pushed back, suggesting that instead policymakers should use this moment to rethink the country’s fundamentally inefficient electricity system, reimagining how rates are designed to begin with and giving federal regulators greater authority to build transmission. “One should not waste a crisis,” he said.     

In today’s political environment, Greenstone’s call for bold thinking can seem a bit out of touch. Congress can barely keep the government open. It’s hard to imagine the body taking on the extremely complex and politically fraught job of reforming the country’s power system. And yet there is a case for thinking bigger—or at the very least laying the groundwork for bigger thinking. 


Right now, the affordability agenda is front of mind and elected officials are responding. In PJM, the Mid Atlantic part of the U.S. grid, officials have implemented a price cap when utilities bid for electricity, even as critics warn the move could discourage new investment. In Indiana, the governor removed the head of the state’s public utility commission after it approved a rate increase. Across the country the political incentive is to keep bills down today even if doing so complicates tomorrow’s reliability challenge. 

 

The system is holding together now. But it’s easy to imagine extreme weather—whether a catastrophic heat wave or deep winter freeze—creating more demand than the system can handle. If demand outstrips supply, rolling blackouts would create a new wave of political anger.     


“I can tell you with absolute certainty that if a grid operator has to choose on the hottest day of summer, whether to send power to a data center to run AI 24/7 or to a residential household that needs air conditioning, it's going to that data center,” says Neil Chatterjee, a former FERC commissioner. “And that's where the pitchforks come out.”


As alarming as pitchforks may be, they also create an opening for a big picture rethinking of how we produce and distribute electricity in the U.S. Indeed, major infrastructure reforms are more likely to happen because the status quo is intolerable than because someone diligently explained the benefits. 

With that in mind, a crisis could unlock much-touted but still elusive permitting reform that makes it easier to build energy infrastructure. It could make the case for a muscular FERC. And I’ve even heard the suggestion that the present moment creates an opportunity to revise the bedrock federal laws that have created challenges in this moment, including the Federal Power Act, the century-old law that governs interstate power transmission. 


The implications of such a move are dramatic. If done right, such reform could be a win for efforts to tackle climate change, given how much clean power has been hampered by a lack of transmission. (And climate advocates could end up being a powerful part of a reform coalition). It would also threaten the utility business model, long dependent on monopolies and state policy. It could be a boon for AI companies that want to move faster, though obviously not everyone would support that. 

A true crisis may be coming soon. It’s unclear who is ready to use it.

item.title: What Octogenarian Pop Divas Show Us About a Life Well-Lived
item.description: Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all in their 80s, show us that conviction outlasts fashion, writes Debbie Millman.

media:content.media:credit: Stewart Cook—CBS/Getty Images; Jason Kempin—Getty Images; Kevin Mazur—BSB/Getty Images; Frank Hoensch—Redferns/Getty Images
media:content.media:description: Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick

item.content:encoded:
On May 20, Cher turned 80 years old. Beyond a celebration of one spectacular career, her birthday is an occasion to consider what it means for a woman to maintain long-term relevance. It opens a larger question about endurance, public scrutiny, and what it takes to live a long, authentic life.

Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all now in their 80s, were criticized for qualities that made them distinctive: being too country, too Jewish, too outspoken, too ambitious, too artificial, too stubborn. Rather than soften those edges, they built careers around them. The traits that once made them targets of ridicule eventually became their signatures.

In a culture that prizes constant reinvention, these octogenarian pop divas suggest another path: longevity through self-definition. They evolved, certainly, but without surrendering the core identities that made them recognizable in the first place. A life well-lived, they remind us, is not the life that pleased the most people, made the fewest demands, or aged into quiet respectability. A good life is one lived on its own terms, refusing every invitation to become smaller, softer, or less fully oneself.

Cher has spent more than six decades in the public eye, moving through music, television, film, fashion, tabloid culture, political commentary, heartbreak, reinvention, ridicule, camp, glamour, and triumph. She’s won a Grammy, an Emmy, an Academy Award, three Golden Globes, and is the only artist to have a number one single on a Billboard chart in seven consecutive decades.

She has been labeled too artificial, too outrageous, too sexual, too blunt, and too much. In the 1970s, her collaboration with Bob Mackie produced dresses that seemed designed to violate every rule of respectable female presentation: sheer, beaded, feathered, midriff-baring, unapologetically theatrical. In 1975, she appeared on the cover of TIME magazine in what was referred to as designer Bob Mackie’s “naked dress,”and in 1986, after being passed over for an Oscar nomination for the movie Mask despite winning Best Actress at Cannes, she arrived at the Academy Awards in a black Mackie ensemble with a towering feathered headdress, a bare midriff, and enough defiance to overwhelm the room. 

The criticism intensified when Cher refused to separate glamour from sexuality as she aged. In 1989, the video for “If I Could Turn Back Time,” filmed aboard the USS Missouri, placed her in a sheer black bodysuit, fishnets, leather jacket, and little else, performing for a cheering crowd of sailors. MTV initially banned the video and later aired it only after 9 p.m. The Navy, which had expected something more conservative, was reportedly embarrassed by the result. What the controversy revealed was not merely discomfort with a costume, but discomfort with a woman in her forties presenting herself as erotic, funny, commanding, and entirely in control of the spectacle.

Through all of it, she never seemed remotely interested in becoming more palatable. At one point in the late 1980s, her body was so scrutinized that there was a debate as to whether or not she had several ribs removed. (She didn’t.) Cher has acknowledged some cosmetic surgery, denied the more lurid inventions, refused the premise that her body required public adjudication, and defiantly stated, “If I want to put my tits on my back, it is nobody’s business but my own.” 

Cher’s dexterity shows up beyond how she survived being mocked for excess. It is revealed by how she transformed excess into architecture. Her costumes, wigs, cosmetic surgery, her public romances, the one-name fame: they constitute the visual and emotional vocabulary she has deftly controlled. Spectacle has never been a mask Cher has hid behind; it is the medium through which she insists on being seen.

This refusal has become Cher’s version of authorship. She has never disappeared into the trope expected of aging women. Instead, she made “too much” the unmistakable, driving force of her power.

Dolly Parton, also 80, spent years being deemed too country, too buxom, too rhinestoned, too blonde, too much of an exaggeration to be taken seriously. Late-night hosts and interviewers repeatedly treated her body as public property and her appearance as a punchline. Johnny Carson joked about her breasts on The Tonight Show; countless others followed the same overly trodden path. 

Parton’s genius was that rather than avoiding the joke, she took control of it. She understood, earlier than almost anyone, that being underestimated could become its own form of power. 

Long before she was appreciated as a national treasure, Parton knew who was really in control of the performance. When she joked that, “it costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” she playfully named the labor, money, intelligence, and craft inside the caricature. Her blonde hair, acrylic nails, high heels, rhinestones, waist-cinching silhouettes, and curves were not accidents of taste. They were the materials of a persona she built deliberately, then protected ferociously. 

Parton turned exaggeration into authorship through repetition and scale. On album covers like Jolene, she presented mountain-girl glamour as a code. In the film 9 to 5, she transformed the image of the underestimated secretary into a working woman with wit, strategy, and rage. At Dollywood, which opened under her name in 1986 near the Tennessee mountains where she was raised, she converted her story into infrastructure: a theme park, a regional employer, a monument to Appalachian storytelling, craft, music, and belonging. What might have been dismissed as kitsch became an economic and cultural engine, directly employing approximately 4,000 people, creating more than 23,000 jobs in the region, and contributing $1.8 billion in annual economic impact to Tennessee.

In the process, Parton became one of the most accomplished songwriters, performers, philanthropists, and entrepreneurs in the world. She has written thousands of songs, including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5,” and “I Will Always Love You,” the latter becoming a rare song that defined two different eras through two different women’s voices. Parton has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, the Country Music Hall of Fame, the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Her Imagination Library, founded in 1995 in honor of her father, who never learned to read or write, has now gifted more than 300 million books to children. The program began in her home county in Tennessee and has grown across multiple countries. 

What makes Parton’s endurance so instructive is that she never abandoned the mountain-girl mythology from which she first emerged. She expanded it. She made it capacious enough to hold country music, film, children’s literacy, vaccine philanthropy, theme parks, baking mixes, fashion, and business. The rhinestones were never a distraction from the seriousness of her work. They were part of the strategy.

The starmaker machinery has long depended on a narrow definition of beauty and controlling the behavior of women. Barbra Streisand, now 84, was told early and often that the things that made her unmistakable were liabilities. She was too Jewish, too nasal, too Brooklyn, too ambitious, too controlling, too unwilling to be remade into someone else’s idea of a star.  

From the start of her career, people told her to fix her nose. In 1964, even this magazine reported as much. In her memoir, she recalls being told by several people that she should get a nose job and have her teeth capped. But she feared that changing her nose might change her voice, and refused, certain that her talent should be enough. 

It was enough, but not before the culture made her pay for it. When Streisand fought to make Yentl, the 1983 film she co-wrote, produced, directed, and starred in, she spent years trying to persuade Hollywood that she could direct it. The film itself is about a Jewish woman who refuses the limits imposed on her mind and disguises herself as a man in order to study, and the parallel was impossible to miss. 

For that insistence, she was often described as “difficult,” a word that frequently means a woman has declined to pretend she has no standards. Streisand has spoken directly about that double standard: a man who asks for a shot to be changed is treated as committed; a woman who asks for the same thing is treated as obsessive. But the very qualities that made her controversial—precision, control, refusal, an almost forensic relationship to detail—also made her work possible.

Dionne Warwick, now 85, offers yet another version of endurance on her own terms. She has been criticized as too direct for those who prefer female softness, too dry for those who mistake composure for distance, and, at various points, judged through racial expectations that flattened the sophistication of her achievement. In 1963, the European record cover featured a white model on the cover of her album, An Empty Place. Her crossover success with Burt Bacharach and Hal David brought her an enormous white audience, but it also exposed her to criticism that her sound was too polished, too restrained, and not sufficiently aligned with what some listeners expected from a Black female singer. 

Warwick’s first hit already contained a declaration of self-possession. In 1962, after learning that “Make It Easy on Yourself,” a song she had hoped would become her first single, had been given to Jerry Butler, she snapped at Bacharach and David, “Don’t make me over.” They turned the phrase into a song. It became Warwick’s first solo hit and, in retrospect, a thesis statement.

Her power has always resided in composure. In songs like “Walk On By,” “Anyone Who Had a Heart,” “I Say a Little Prayer,” and “A House Is Not a Home,” Warwick sang with elegance, intelligence, and restraint. “Walk On By,” released in 1964, is a devastating song precisely because she refuses to overperform devastation. The lyric asks an old lover to keep walking if they see her breaking down; Warwick sings it as though dignity itself is the last remaining shelter. In her performances, she commanded the room by withholding exactly enough.

In recent years, Warwick has also become beloved by younger generations for the directness that has defined her public persona. On Twitter (now X) she began asking questions with the kind of plainspoken authority that felt almost radical in a culture addicted to irony. Why, she asked Chance the Rapper, did he need to include “the Rapper” in his name if he was very obviously a rapper? She wondered publicly about The Weeknd’s spelling. The exchange with Chance the Rapper eventually led to a collaboration, but the larger revelation was that Warwick had not become newly direct. New audiences had simply discovered the clarity that had always been there.

She does not appear to be chasing relevance so much as allowing new audiences to catch up. That distinction matters: there is a difference between remaining visible because one is desperate to be relevant and remaining visible because one is confident in their own skin. Warwick’s authority comes from that confidence.

None of these superstars survived and thrived by becoming less themselves, and this is what makes their continued cultural relevance so instructive. They teach us that to age successfully and gracefully, we need not reinvent ourselves, but rather to know who we are and to evolve.  

Make no mistake; these octogenarians have certainly evolved. Cher moved from folk-pop duo to television star to Oscar-winning actress to dance-floor futurist to Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductee and memoirist. Parton moved from the Porter Wagoner Show to pop crossover to film to Dollywood to global philanthropy. Streisand moved from nightclub singer to Broadway phenomenon to film star to director, producer, and author. Warwick moved from the Scepter Records years to global pop elegance to activist, survivor, internet oracle, and elder stateswoman of direct address.

But for each of these women, adapting to new stages and industries has been conducted on their own terms, without compromising the essence of who they have always been. Their careers were built on deepening their commitments to themselves until the very qualities once deemed excessive became iconic.

Women are often instructed to age by diminishing. They are instructed, both explicitly and implicitly, to gracefully accept less attention, less power, less sexuality, less ambition, and less contradiction. They are praised for aging gracefully (which usually means aging quietly and out of sight). They are expected to become wiser but not louder, visible but not vain, accomplished but not demanding, and well-preserved but not provocative. Even admiration can become a form of containment, turning older women into monuments rather than allowing them to be monumental. 

Cher, Parton, Streisand, and Warwick have resisted these strictures. They have not aged into neutrality. Pop divas in their 80s show us that conviction outlasts fashion. They made new work, took risks, changed formats, survived failures, and were undeterred. They did so without compromising the traits that made them singular. 

At a moment when many people feel pressured to change themselves to meet the expectations of others, these octogenarian icons offer a different model of a life well-lived: one built not on perpetual reinvention, but on the courage to remain unmistakably oneself.

A life well-lived, they remind us, is not the life that pleased the most people, made the fewest demands, or aged into quiet respectability. A good life is one lived on its own terms, refusing every invitation to become smaller, softer, or less fully oneself.
