item.title: What Is Pickaxe Mountain, Iran’s Underground Nuclear Site That Trump Is Threatening?
item.description: An expert tells TIME why the underground facility is at the center of much debate.

media:content.media:description: Vantor satellite image shows an overview of Natanz nuclear site and adjacent Pickaxe Mountain mining area in Isfahan Province, Iran, on Nov. 14, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
Amid the resumption of the Iran war, President Donald Trump has again threatened to attack sites linked to Iran’s nuclear program.

Last week, Trump was asked if he believes Iran has moved nuclear centrifuges into Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near one of the country's primary enrichment facilities.

“They may have, we don’t have it on record,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday. “It doesn’t mean anything unless they have the material [uranium]. We follow the material, that’s where the action is.”

“We’ll be hitting that area, probably pretty soon, and there’s not a thing they can do about it,” he added. "Any site where they’re even thinking about nuclear, we’ll be hitting it very powerfully."

Trump had previously threatened the Iranian facility during a July 13 podcast interview when he declared: “We're going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready."

The President received vocal support for his renewed focus on the site over the weekend. Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said during a TV interview he thinks the U.S. "ought to bomb Pickaxe Mountain and try to reach what's underneath it."

The resumption of the Iran war on July 7, just weeks after the signing of the interim cease-fire agreement, has largely focused on the continued struggle over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade passage between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. But there is also renewed focus on Iran’s nuclear capabilities, as Trump has repeatedly stated that Tehran must never be allowed to build or procure a nuclear weapon.

Amid the escalating threats and tensions, here’s what to know about Pickaxe Mountain, known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La. 

What is Pickaxe Mountain?

The underground site is situated around 220 km (140 ‌miles) south of Tehran and 2 km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz nuclear complex.

In June last year, the U.S. joined Israel in launching strikes on three key Iranian nuclear sites—an action Trump said had “completely and totally obliterated” the targeted facilities.

Natanz was among the facilities hit, as it was believed to house highly-enriched uranium. The entrances to the nuclear site were targeted again in the early days of the Iran war which started on Feb. 28.

During last year's 12-day war, the nuclear facility outside the city of Isfahan, about 80 miles away, was also bombed. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has said tunnels at that facility is likely where a cache of some 970 pounds of enriched uranium are being stored.

According to the U.S.-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS), the tunnel facility under construction at Pickaxe Mountain has not been previously targeted in either June 2025 or the 2026 war, “aside from the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile, which we believe was most likely associated with air defense.”

Construction of the Pickaxe Mountain facility started in 2020, after a fire at Natanz, which Iran's nuclear body argued had been caused by an act of sabotage.

Iran at the time said the underground halls were intended to replace the destroyed above-ground advanced centrifuge assembly facility at the Natanz site, according to ISIS.

“It's a very deep facility. We don't know exactly how deep, but it's very likely at least 100 meters deep,” James Acton, co-director of the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, tells TIME.

The highly-fortified site would be a difficult target for the U.S., experts say.

“There's just no way to destroy this facility. The best one can do is try to collapse the tunnel entrances," explains Acton.

Is Pickaxe Mountain a functioning site?

Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. is watching Pickaxe Mountain “closely" and doesn't see any activity there.

ISIS’ assessment, based on satellite imagery, is that the facility is not yet operational, but construction continues.

The think tank said it “remains unclear when Pickaxe Mountain could be operational… It is also unclear if Iran still plans on installing a large-scale assembly facility, given the destruction of Iran’s centrifuge program, including Iran’s ability to make centrifuge components needed for an assembly plant.”

Esmail Baghaei, spokesperson for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, has said there is no nuclear action at the site, insisting any of Iran’s nuclear activities have “been fully declared to the IAEA, in accordance with its safeguards obligations.”

“Washington’s obsessive focus on Kolang Kouh, where no nuclear activity is taking place, is nothing more than a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage,” he said on July 22.

If Iran starts to rebuild its centrifuge manufacturing capability, “it could plan to install a smaller centrifuge assembly facility in Pickaxe Mountain able to serve a nuclear weapons program,” according to ISIS.

Acton tells TIME it remains a "legitimate concern” that Pickaxe Mountain could potentially be used for “more than just secure storage.”

“The concern is, whether or not it was developed as an enrichment plant, the fear is now that it would be used as one,” he says.

Rafael Grossi, chief of the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog IAEA, told PBS in March that Iran had previously “announced its intention to have nuclear activity” at Pickaxe Mountain, referring to it as “part of their quite systematic intention to put their most sensitive facilities underground.”

Grossi said the IAEA inspectors had not been granted access to the Pickaxe Mountain site.

Additionally, the nuclear watchdog has been unable to independently verify Iran’s centrifuge capacity and production since 2021, so Tehran may have reserves despite strikes over the last two years.

With the destruction of Iran’s other centrifuge related facilities, “the Pickaxe Mountain complex is a potential candidate site for any Iranian reconstitution of its centrifuge program, from centrifuge component production to centrifuge assembly to uranium enrichment,” ISIS stated in November 2025.

Trump's nuclear row with Iran

Shortly before the U.S. military conducted its 13th consecutive evening of strikes against Iran on Thursday, Trump again accused Tehran of having “evil intentions” and insisted “we cannot let them, ever, even think about having a nuclear weapon.”

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei in April vowed to protect its nuclear and missile capabilities in direct defiance of Trump. He said his country will defend its “fundamental and modern technologies—from nano and bio to nuclear and missile—as their national capital and will guard them like their maritime, land, and air borders.”

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is “peaceful,” but concerns remain among Western leaders.


The Memorandum of Understanding signed on June 17 asserts that Iran can never develop a nuclear weapon—a promise the regime has made in the past. The agreement states that the U.S. and Iran will address Iran’s existing stockpile of enriched material, “with the minimum methodology to be down blending on site” under the supervision of inspectors with the IAEA.

It also said both countries had “acknowledged the critical importance of the nuclear issues… and expressed their intention to immediately address these issues in the negotiations in order to achieve mutual agreement on them.”

The interim agreement laid out the terms of an extended 60-day cease-fire to allow time for technical talks to take place. That deadline is set to expire in mid-August, but the resumption of the war has brought the entire deal into question.

item.title: Trump Will Give ‘Unifying Yet Vicious’ Speech at Rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner, White House Says
item.description: After the shooting at the April event, Trump revealed that he had intended to rip into the media during his speech, but would now likely not do so.

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump speaks at Wheeler High School in Marietta, Georgia, on July 22, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump will be giving a “unifying yet vicious” speech at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner on Friday evening, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt previewed.

“The President’s speech will be a combination of unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious, all at the same time, if you can imagine that,” Leavitt told NBC News. “One thing I can assure you, it will be entertaining.”

Last month, the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) announced that it was rescheduling its annual dinner to July 24, after its event in April was disrupted by a gunman who charged a security checkpoint at the venue and exchanged fire with law enforcement before he was apprehended.

“The White House Correspondents’ Dinner has served as a celebration of a free press and the vital role of journalism in our democracy for over a century,” WHCA President Weijia Jiang said in a letter to association members last month. “When gunfire interrupted this year’s event, it further clarified the WHCA’s mission to advocate for the freedoms that are protected in the First Amendment.”

“We will not allow an act of violence to have the last word,” she continued.

Jiang said at the time that the July dinner “will feature significantly enhanced safety measures and new access procedures,” and that the event “will be a more intimate gathering.”

The WHCA also announced earlier this week that it will present an award to Secret Service Police Officer Victor Gonzales, who the Secret Service said "heroically engaged the armed suspect, placing himself directly in harm's way” and ended up being “struck in his protective vest.”

“Officer Gonzales played a significant role when he ran toward danger so that thousands of others could make it home safely,” Jiang said in a statement. “His courage stemmed from a dedication to service, which we are looking forward to honoring this week.”

The WHCA said that it would also award the staff of the Washington Hilton, the venue for the April dinner, with the same special recognition at the rescheduled event.

“Even after the men and women of the Washington Hilton experienced a harrowing situation, they continued to take care of guests,” Jiang said. “The WHCA appreciates their professionalism and commitment to service, which was on full display on April 25th. Every member of the team deserves to be recognized for their dedication.”

Trump applauded the WHCA last month for rescheduling the event, calling it “a sign of Strength and Fortitude,” and added that he had once again been invited to speak. The April dinner that was interrupted by gunfire was the first time that Trump, who has had a contentious relationship with the press, had attended the Correspondents’ Dinner as President.

After the shooting in April, Trump revealed that he had initially intended to rip into the media during his speech at the event, but that he would likely not do so now.

“I don’t know if I could ever be as rough as I was going to be tonight,” he said after the Washington Hilton was evacuated the night of the shooting. “I think I’m going to be probably very nice. I’ll be very boring the next time, but we’re going to have a great event.”

After the WHCA announced the rescheduled dinner in June, Trump again suggested that his speech may not be as harsh as the one he planned to deliver in April.

“I don’t know whether or not I will give the same rather nasty statements, at least as it concerns certain people, but we will soon find out,” he said on Truth Social. “In any event, it will be a ‘HOT’ ticket!”

item.title: How to Know If You’re Eligible for a Piece of the $2.5 Billion Amazon Prime Settlement, and How to File a Claim
item.description: The deadline to submit a claim for compensation under the historic settlement is fast approaching.

media:content.media:description: Low-angle view of the side of a blue trailer semi truck with the logo for Amazon Prime in San Ramon, California, on October 8, 2018.

item.content:encoded:
The deadline is fast approaching for eligible Amazon Prime subscribers to file a claim to receive a portion of a historic $2.5 billion settlement the company reached with the Federal Trade Commission.

Amazon agreed to the deal last September to settle a lawsuit over allegations that “millions of customers into “unknowingly” enrolling in its paid Amazon Prime service and then made the subscriptions difficult to cancel. 

The settlement requires Amazon to stop those alleged practices and pay heft fines—as well as offering “full relief for the estimated 35 million consumers impacted by unwanted Prime enrollment or deferred cancellation.”

Amazon has denied any wrong-doing. 

"Amazon and our executives have always followed the law and this settlement allows us to move forward and focus on innovating for customers,” the company said in a statement following the settlement announcement. “We work incredibly hard to make it clear and simple for customers to both sign up or cancel their Prime membership, and to offer substantial value for our many millions of loyal Prime members around the world.”

The deadline for submitting a claim for compensation under the settlement is July 27.

Here’s how to know if you’re eligible for a portion of the settlement, and how to file a claim. 

Who's eligible?

To be eligible for a refund under the settlement, you must be an AmazonPrime customer in the U.S. who “unintentionally” signed up for the service through a “challenged enrollment flow” or attempted to cancel your subscription but were unable to between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025. 

According to the FTC, the challenged enrollment flows include the universal Amazon Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, and the Prime Video enrollment flow. The agency noted that customers do not have to determine for themselves whether they signed up for Prime through one of those flows; Amazon will make that determination.

You are also only eligible for the settlement if you have used no more than three of Prime’s benefits, such as Prime Video or Prime Music, within any 12-month period after you enrolled in the service.

How to submit a claim

Eligible Amazon customers should have received a notice to file their claim by email or mail, according to the settlement website. 

Using a “Claim ID and PIN” included in the notice they received, customers can also access their claim form via the settlement website. There is also an option to file a claim through the website without those details contained in the notice. 

The claim form asks customers to provide their name, current address, and zip code, and to specify whether they were "unintentionally enrolled” in Prime or were unable to cancel during the designated time period. 

No documents are required to answer those questions, nor to prove whether you used Prime benefits during a 12-month period. 

Unlike private settlements, customers do not have the option to opt-out of government settlements like this one. 

The website advises customers to contact admin@SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com for further support. 

How much compensation will claimants receive?

Eligible Prime customers will get a refund of their Prime fees, up to a maximum of $51.

Amazon expects to send out payments in late 2026.
